chapters.label: Prologue
chapters.title: Ice Storm
chapters.html:
I am sitting here with a pocket watch in my hand.

It is small and heavy and worn smooth at the edges, the way metal gets when it has lived for years in a man's pocket and been taken out a thousand times to check the hour. I open the case. Inside there is one word: Edinburgh. That is almost all he left me.

The watch belonged to my grandfather. The family says he carried it across the Atlantic in 1929, and he carried it for the rest of his life, and he died before I was born. I am named for him. And for most of my life I knew almost nothing about him: a name, a few photographs, a grave in Cranston, a handful of stories my mother told about a quiet man who dressed shop windows and loved to read.

Who was he? Where did he come from? Why was there only one word inside his watch?

So I went searching for him, back through time, through ships' manifests and city streets and a century of other people's lives, until, in my own mind and heart, I brought him back to life.

This is what I found.

On the last day of his life, Rhode Island was icing over.

The storm came up the coast in the dark. At T. F. Green Airport in Warwick, the weather station that served Providence, the strongest gust of Thursday, March 9, 1961, was recorded at 4:12 in the morning: thirty-three miles an hour out of the southeast. Over the course of the day the station logged fog, snow, sleet, glaze and rain. Its thermometer ranged between thirty-one and forty-two degrees, and its gauge caught a little more than an inch of precipitation for the day.

It was the seventh week of the Kennedy administration. In many Catholic homes in Providence the new President's photograph was already on the wall. Five weeks later, on April 12, a Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin would become the first man to orbit the earth.

Providence was changing. The mills that had made Rhode Island rich were closing or moving south. The new interstate highway was being cut through the city. Downtown, where he had dressed windows before the war, was losing its shoppers to the new plazas out on the suburban highways, with their big parking lots and their glass fronts lit all night. Congress had authorized a hurricane barrier at Fox Point, at the head of the bay, so that the sea could never again do to downtown what it had done in 1938.

That day, at St. Joseph's Hospital, Laurence Brown Douglas died. He was fifty-three years old. The illness had been brief. My mother remembered that the family did not know he had lung cancer until he was in the hospital.

He lived at 644 River Avenue, in the Elmhurst section of Providence, with his wife, Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas, a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. Before he went into business for himself he had dressed windows for Bond Stores, the clothing chain, in San Francisco and been its display manager in Pittsburgh. In the last years of his life he was dressing windows on his own account; the city directory of 1960 listed him as displayman for Carter's Men Store in Pawtucket.

On Saturday the Pawtucket Times ran his obituary on page three. It said he had been born in Edinburgh, Scotland. It named his parents as the late Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. It said that for the past fifteen years he had dressed windows for Pawtucket firms. It listed his wife, three daughters, and a sister in Chicago.

Most of it was true as far as it went. None of it told how he began.

He had been born in Edinburgh fifty-three years earlier to a twenty-one-year-old domestic servant who was not married and who did not raise him. No father was entered in the register. She was not Elizabeth Douglas. She did not give him the name Douglas. On the day his birth was written into the register, his name was Lawrence Brown.

He would carry that name across the Atlantic. He would carry another one through a Scottish schoolroom, a Chicago wedding and a federal courthouse in Pittsburgh. By the end he had put the two together, Laurence Brown Douglas, and kept them both. The records spell his first name both ways. This book calls him Laurence, the spelling he used as a man, and keeps Lawrence wherever a record wrote it that way.

This is the story of how he came by those names, and of the people who gave them to him.

It begins in the Scottish Borders, more than a century before that March day, with a family of farm laborers who owned nothing but their skill.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: Other Men's Land
chapters.html:
Every life has a beginning before it begins. His began in a ploughed field, behind a pair of horses, on land that no one in his family had ever owned.

The Browns worked other men's land.

They lived through one of the great upheavals in the history of the Scottish countryside. In the century before 1850 the old run-rig farms, worked in common by whole townships, had been swept away and replaced by large enclosed farms let to single tenants, who paid rent to the laird and hired labor by the half-year. The cottars and small tenants who had once held a scrap of land of their own became landless hired men. A ploughman of the 1840s owned his skill, his strength and perhaps a chest of clothes. He did not own the roof over his head; the cottage came with the job, and when the job ended at the term he loaded his family and furniture onto a farm cart and moved.

He was paid partly in money and partly in kind: so many bolls of oatmeal, so many hundredweights of potatoes, a row in the potato field, the keep of a cow, coals carted from the nearest pit. Oatmeal porridge in the morning, brose at noon, potatoes and milk at night: it was a hard diet, but in the Lowlands it was regular, and the Lowland farm worker was spared the famine that the potato blight of 1846 brought to the Highlands and to Ireland.

He dressed for work and weather: a coarse linen shirt, a waistcoat and jacket of thick homespun, moleskin or corduroy trousers tied below the knee with the straps called nicky-tams, heavy boots studded with iron nails, and a flat blue bonnet. His wife wore a long dark skirt, a coarse apron, a shawl crossed over her breast, and a white linen cap, the mutch, on her hair. On Sunday he put on a black coat kept for the kirk and for funerals, and she a better shawl and a bonnet.

They came from the high, bare sheep country of Peeblesshire, in the Scottish Borders, where the Tweed rises in the hills above Tweedsmuir and runs east through Stobo and Lyne toward the market town of Peebles. William Brown, born about 1835, was a ploughman. He walked behind a pair of horses, turning the stony ground for oats and turnips, and he moved from farm to farm as the hiring fairs and the term days dictated.

His wife was Agnes McGarth, born about 1840 at Tweedsmuir. The McGarths were hill people. In 1851 the census found her father, Tweedie McGarth, about thirty-eight, and her mother, Jane, about forty-one, a woman from Wamphray in Dumfriesshire, with a house full of children: Jane, Agnes, James Tweedie, Sarah, Ann and Janet. The family's names would outlast the family. "Tweedie" and "McGarth" were passed down as middle names for three generations, a way of remembering who you came from when you owned nothing else to leave.

William and Agnes Brown had at least ten children. There was William, about 1859. There was Lawrence Tweedie Brown, born on September 14, 1860, in Peebles. There was George, born on July 18, 1862. Then Alexander, Jane, John, James Tweedie, a daughter Agnes born at Stobo about 1875, Thomas, and Tweedie McGarth Brown about 1880. In 1871 the census found Lawrence, ten, and George, eight, living in the same household.

Two of those boys matter to this story.

Lawrence Tweedie Brown would grow up, marry a woman named Isabella Graham from Cambusnethan, raise a family at Traquair and Sanquhar, and eventually settle in Quebec. He died in 1943. Forty-seven years after his own birth, his niece would give his name to her son.

George was that niece's father. He became a ploughman like his own father. He did not live long enough to become anything else.

The songs they knew were the old ones. On winter nights in the bothies, the bare stone sheds where unmarried ploughmen slept, the men sang the bothy ballads of their own lives: songs about mean farmers, bad meal, cold beds and the girls at the next farm. Robert Burns, the "ploughman poet," who had followed the plough himself on his father's farms, had been dead nearly forty years when William Brown was born, and a cottage that owned two books was likely to own the Bible and Burns.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: A Ploughman's Daughter
chapters.html:
She was born in a ploughman's cottage, a week before Christmas, in the dark of a Border winter.

George Brown married Christina Henderson on Friday, June 1, 1883, in the parish of Libberton, at Quothquan, in the upper valley of the River Clyde. He was twenty. She was twenty-three.

Rural Scotland in the 1880s was emptying. Machines were coming onto the farms: horse-drawn reapers and binders, threshing mills driven by steam. Each one did the work of several men. Every year thousands of farm servants left for the coalfields of Lanarkshire, the shipyards and engine shops of Glasgow, or the emigrant ships for Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Those who stayed were better paid than their fathers had been, and better fed, but they were still hired by the half-year and still lived in houses they did not own.

The Hendersons were Libberton people. Christina's father, Alexander Henderson, born about 1830, and her mother, Jane Robb, had raised a family there: Christina, born on March 19, 1860, then Jane, Janet, David, and in about 1876 a late son, Andrew. The parish was farm country on the north side of the Clyde, four miles from the market town of Biggar, under a bald round hill called Quothquan Law. Across the river, filling the southwest sky, stood Tinto, the red hill of Clydesdale, with a great cairn on its summit that people said had been carried up stone by stone as penance.

Eleven weeks after the wedding, at twenty past eight on the morning of Saturday, August 18, 1883, Christina gave birth to a daughter at Quothquan. She went to the registrar herself on September 5 and gave the child's name as Mary Henderson Brown.

By the winter of 1885 George had found work across the county line, at Edston, a farm in the parish of Lyne, a few miles west of Peebles. The farm cottages there, low and stone-built with slate roofs, still stand along the road. At half past two in the afternoon on Friday, December 18, 1885, Christina gave birth to a second daughter.

On the last day of the year George registered her at Peebles. The registrar, George Morison, wrote the entry on page 50 of his book, number 149: Agnes McGarth Brown, female, born December eighteenth, 2h 30m p.m., at Edston, Peebles. Father, George Brown, ploughman. Mother, Christina Brown, maiden surname Henderson. Parents married 1883 June 1st, Libberton, Lanark. George signed as father.

He gave his daughter his own mother's name, Agnes McGarth. The registrar wrote "McGarth" with a capital M and a small raised c, the way Scots clerks wrote it then. More than a century later an indexer would print "MCGRATH" across the top of the scanned page, and that spelling would follow her through the indexes. The handwriting says McGarth.

George Brown died at Edston at half past one in the morning on Monday, April 5, 1886, when his younger daughter was three and a half months old. He was twenty-three years old. His death register is the document that names his own parents, William Brown, ploughman, and Agnes Brown, maiden surname McGarth.

Christina was left a widow at twenty-six, with a girl of two and a half and a baby of three and a half months. She took them home to Libberton.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Row Called Castle
chapters.html:
In a row of six stone cottages that the village called Castle, a little girl of five was growing up among old men and widows.

On the road out of Quothquan village, past the smithy, there was a row of six crofters' cottages that the village called Castle.

For a girl of five like Agnes, the world was the length of the village road. Children walked to school, came home to help in the house and the fields, and by twelve or thirteen were expected to start earning. A farm laborer's daughter could expect to go into service, in a farmhouse kitchen or a big house, while she was still in her early teens.

In the first cottage lived John Mather, a crofter of seventy, and his wife, Margaret. In the second lived George Weir, seventy-five, the parish mole catcher, and his wife, Jane. In the third lived the widow Ann Archibald, fifty-four, with her daughter Mary, twenty-seven, her son Alexander, twenty, who broke stones for the county roads, and her son John, seventeen, a farm servant. In the fourth, alone, lived Janet Paterson, seventy-eight, on the parish roll as a pauper. In the sixth lived old Christina Henderson, ninety-four, living on her own means with her daughter and a granddaughter.

The fifth house was crowded. It was the home of Jane Henderson, fifty-six, Christina Brown's mother, a crofter born in Carnwath. With her lived her daughter Jane, twenty-seven, a dressmaker; her son Andrew, a schoolboy; and a young farm laborer of eighteen named James Parker.

James Parker had been born in Biggar. He had come into the Henderson house as a small boy, and the census had a word for what he was. In 1881, when he was eight and at school, the enumerator wrote him down as "Adopted Son". In 1891 he was "Adopted". His marriage register later named Benjamin Parker and Jane Lawson as his parents. How he came to the Hendersons remains unknown. One family tree later called him James Parker Henderson, a son of the house, but it gave no evidence, and no census called him anything but adopted.

On the night of Sunday, April 5, 1891, the census taker found two more children in the fifth house: Jane Henderson's granddaughters, Mary Brown, seven, and Agnes Brown, five.

They were there because their mother was dead. Christina Brown had died at Quothquan on February 10, 1891, eight weeks before the census. She was thirty. Her name was cut into the Henderson family stone.

The year was not finished with the row. On June 8, 1891, the girls' grandmother, Jane Henderson, died too. Twelve days later, on June 20, the Archibalds buried their son John, eighteen.

So by midsummer of 1891, Agnes Brown was five and a half years old and had lost her father, her mother and the grandmother who had taken her in. What she had left was her sister, her uncle Andrew, her aunt Jane, and the boy the family called adopted.

Agnes grew up in a household where a child who was not born to it could be taken in and kept. Twenty-one years later, a Dunfermline school clerk would write the same word, Adopted, beside her own son's name.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The New Laird
chapters.html:
A rich man bought the land under the village, and the village began to change.

In 1898 the land under the village changed hands.

For generations the Chancellor family had owned the Shieldhill estate, a rambling mansion built around an old tower above Quothquan, and with it the village and its cottages. The Chancellors buried their dead in the ruined old kirk at Quothquan, which they had taken as a family burial place around 1780. In 1898 they sold to Nathaniel Dunlop, a Glasgow shipowner of the Allan Line and chairman of the Clyde Navigation Trust. Dunlop rebuilt Huntfield Place, turning six houses into four, and enlarged the smith's house. He was rich, Presbyterian and energetic. In 1903 he and his daughter, Miss Ellen Dunlop, put up Shieldhill Hall in the village, a cross-shaped hall of corrugated iron with timber gables and an open porch, for evening services. It still stands.

Money from the Atlantic paid for the new Shieldhill. The Allan Line, which Nathaniel Dunlop had served for half a century, ran steamers from Glasgow to Quebec and Montreal and carried tens of thousands of Scottish emigrants to Canada. The same ships that paid for the laird's improvements would carry the village's children away.

By the census of March 31, 1901, the Castle row had new names. The enumerator came first to Gean Tree Cottages. Gean is the Scots word for the wild cherry, a tree that flowers white in April and ripens its small dark fruit in July. At schedule 13 lived Mary Archibald, thirty-five, a sewing mistress. At schedule 14 lived James Grossart, eighty, a road surfaceman born at Carstairs, with his granddaughter Marion, twenty-two.

At schedule 15 was Lime Tree Cottage, and the Hendersons.

The head of the house was now Andrew Henderson, twenty-five, a groom. Long after he was gone the village would remember "Andrew Henderson, late of Lime Tree" as a poet and a keeper of bees. James Parker, twenty-eight, still lived with him, no longer called adopted but a boarder, and working now as a gamekeeper. With them were Andrew's two nieces: Mary Brown, seventeen, and Agnes Brown, fifteen.

There was no grown woman left in the house. The aunt, Jane the dressmaker, had gone.

Up the hill, Shieldhill House stood nearly empty on census night. Dunlop was at his house in Govan. The estate was kept by resident staff: servants, gardeners and keepers. Mary Archibald's brother Alexander, thirty, was now the domestic gardener there. At the neighboring estate of Huntfield the gamekeeper, Robert Arthur, lived at the lodge. Another keeper, Robert Clarkson, lived at Cormiston. The census does not say which estate James Parker kept game for.

James Parker stayed in the district. By 1911 he was married, with three children, and keeping game at Shieldhill Mains (Chapter 12).

Agnes, at fifteen, was a girl of the row with no parents and no money. For a girl like that in Upper Clydesdale the likeliest work was service. By the summer of 1907 the register would call her a domestic servant.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: The Woman Who Would Raise Him
chapters.html:
She was four years old when her mother sailed for the other side of the world without her.

Thirty miles away, on the southern edge of Edinburgh, lived the woman who would raise Agnes Brown's son. She had begun life as he would: born to an unmarried servant, with no father named, and raised by others.

The south side of Edinburgh in the 1870s was not the city of the guidebooks. Beyond the Meadows and the new villas of Grange and Newington, the road ran out through Liberton and Gilmerton into a country of coal pits, limeworks and miners' rows. Men went down shafts under the fields to cut coal for the city's fires; women and girls worked at the pithead and in the fields; children worked as soon as they could. The Old Town itself, a few miles to the north, was among the most crowded places in Europe. Whole families lived in single rooms in the tall tenements off the High Street and the Cowgate, and the Improvement Act of 1867 had only begun to pull down the worst closes.

Elizabeth Millar McDonald was born on May 31, 1874, at Liberton. Her mother, Ann McDonald, was about twenty and unmarried. The birth record names Ann and no one else. There is no father.

Two years later, on July 28, 1876, Ann married a laborer named Robert Alexander Hope at 33 Regent Park Square in Glasgow. Robert Hope had been born at Rigg, near Gretna, on July 14, 1852. His mother's name was Elizabeth Millar.

Emigration offered a way out, and in the 1870s New Zealand wanted settlers badly. Its government paid assisted passages for working families from Britain, and thousands of Scots took them, in sailing ships that took about three months to reach Otago and Canterbury. In 1878 Ann and Robert Hope sailed. Their son, John Rakaia Hope, was born at sea on September 26, 1878, and was named for the emigrant ship. They settled at Cross Creek in the Wairarapa and raised four more children there. Ann died at Cross Creek in 1915. Robert died at Pukekohe in 1930.

They did not take Lizzie. She was four.

She was raised by her grandparents, John McDonald, a man of the Gilmerton district, and his wife, Janet, born Janet Page. In 1881 the census found them on the Main Road at Gilmerton: John, fifty-two; Janet, fifty-two; their grown son George; a daughter, Janet; a son, Alexander; and Elizabeth, six, a scholar, entered as "Grandchild".

At sixteen she was in service. On the night of the 1891 census she was living in as a general domestic servant at 14 Wilson Road, Liberton, in the house of a Robert and Mary Dryder and their four small sons, the youngest eight months old. Another servant, Catherine Davidson, twenty-eight, lived in with her.

Like her mother, and like the girl in Clydesdale whose son she would raise, Lizzie McDonald was a servant.

On June 9, 1899, at 34 St Patrick Square in Edinburgh, she married Robert Douglas, by the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. The marriage register gives her age as twenty-four, a domestic servant living at 4 Hatton Place. He was twenty-three, a saw miller of 29 St Leonard's Terrace, the son of Archibald Douglas, a forester, and Isabella Douglas, born Isabella Gray. Robert had been born on May 8, 1876, at 9 Canon Street in Edinburgh, when his father was a traveller for a wood merchant. His parents had married in January 1863 in the parish of Newton, on the southeastern edge of the city, close to Liberton and Gilmerton, the country Lizzie came from. The Douglases, like the McDonalds, were Edinburgh people. For her own parents Lizzie gave the names of the grandparents who had raised her, John McDonald, coal salesman, and Janet McDonald, born Page. One of the two witnesses was Janet Page Moodie. Within two years Robert was working as a stone machineman, a skilled worker who cut and dressed stone by machine. On April 29, 1900, Lizzie gave birth to a daughter and named her Janet Page Douglas, after the grandmother who had raised her.

On census night, March 31, 1901, the young family lived at 5 Beaumont Place, in the tenements of Newington on Edinburgh's south side: Robert, twenty-four; Lizzie, twenty-six; and Janet, eleven months.

Family information says that Robert and Lizzie had a second daughter, Isabella Gray Douglas, named for Robert's mother, and that she died as an infant.

There is no evidence that the Douglases of Beaumont Place and the Browns of Lime Tree Cottage had ever heard of each other.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: The Term Days
chapters.html:
It happened in the year of the harvest heat wave, in the farm country of the upper Clyde. Who the father was, no record tells.

In the Upper Ward of Lanarkshire a servant's year turned on two days. Whitsunday, fixed by law at May 28, and Martinmas, fixed at November 28, were the term days. On those days engagements ended and began, wages were paid out for the half-year, and servants who were moving on carried their boxes out to a cart. A girl hired at Whitsunday usually lived in, ate in her employer's kitchen, and was paid at Martinmas. The government's Labour Gazette put the going rate for women farm servants in the southwest of Scotland at seven to ten pounds a half-year, with board. In 1906 it noted that women willing to go into service were hard to find.

For a young unmarried woman, the moral world was older and harder. In the Scotland of 1906 a pregnancy outside marriage was a disgrace to the girl and to her family, though not always to the man. In the countryside it was also common: illegitimate births in rural Scotland ran well above the English rate, and in some farming counties of the northeast and southwest about one child in ten was born to an unmarried mother. The kirk session no longer called women before the congregation to be rebuked, as it had a generation or two earlier, but a servant who was found to be pregnant could lose her place at the next term and her character with it.

Agnes Brown turned twenty in December 1905. Where she worked in 1906 is not recorded.

The summer ended in a heat wave. At Leith, on the Firth of Forth, the Met Office's reporting station recorded highs climbing through the last days of August: seventy-six degrees, then seventy-seven, then eighty. In the twenty-four hours that ended at eight o'clock on the morning of Saturday, September 1, the Leith thermometer reached eighty-five, and it already stood at sixty-six at the morning reading. The official report noted that across the south and east of Scotland the afternoon highs had gone above eighty.

The harvest stood in that heat. In the fields of the upper Clyde the oats were cut and set up in stooks to dry. Partridge shooting opened on September 1, and on the estates around Quothquan the keepers were out with the guns.

Somewhere in those weeks, between about the first week of September and the middle of October 1906, Agnes Brown conceived a child. She was twenty.

On the farms of the Upper Ward the young people still met at the feeing fairs, the harvest dances and the kirk door. The bicycle had given country boys and girls a freedom their parents had never had: a farm lad could ride ten miles to a dance on a Saturday night and be back for the morning milking.

Martinmas fell on Wednesday, November 28, 1906. Where Agnes spent it, no record says.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Road to Edinburgh
chapters.html:
Her son would be born in the capital, thirty miles from home.

Whitsunday 1907 fell on a Tuesday. At Leith it was a cold day for the end of May: an east wind off the North Sea, a high of about fifty-two degrees, and a clear night that fell to thirty-seven. By then her child was due within weeks. A servant in that condition rarely kept a place where she lived in. Whether she left at the term, or before it, no one wrote down.

For an unmarried country girl there was a well-worn way to have a baby out of sight of her own parish, and it led to Edinburgh. Agnes's son would be born there in the middle of June.

Edinburgh in 1907 was a city of about three hundred and twenty thousand people, the capital of a country without a parliament: the seat of the law courts, the Church of Scotland, the banks, the universities and the great medical school. It was also, behind the grand fronts of Princes Street and the New Town, a city of deep poverty. About a third of its families lived in one or two rooms, and the death rate in the Old Town closes was far higher than in the villas a mile away.

No record says how she traveled. Quothquan had no station. The nearest was Thankerton, across the Clyde, about a mile and a half by road. The railway had come through in 1848. The Carlisle expresses ran through without stopping; the local trains stopped. On a timetable from 1900 a morning train left Thankerton at 8:35 and reached Edinburgh at 9:40, and an afternoon train left at 2:35 and arrived at 3:55. At the parliamentary rate of a penny a mile, the third-class fare would have come to about two shillings and eightpence for the thirty-two miles: for a country servant, something like half a week's wages.

The line ran north up the Clyde valley to Carstairs Junction, where it divided for Glasgow and Edinburgh, then climbed northeast onto the moor, past Carnwath, where Agnes's grandmother had been born, past Auchengray and Cobbinshaw, where it ran beside the reservoir that fed the Union Canal, and past Harburn and Midcalder. Then it came down into the farmland of Midlothian, with the long ridge of the Pentland Hills to the south, past Curriehill and Slateford, where the canal crossed the Water of Leith on its aqueduct, and into the city.

The Caledonian line ended at Princes Street Station, at the west end of Princes Street. Lauriston Place lay about three-quarters of a mile to the south. It was a street of institutions and small shops: Chalmers Hospital at number 55; the Lauriston Place United Free church at 77; the Royal Maternity Hospital at 79, with its own telephone line, number 837. Across the street, at number 118, beside George Carse the painter's shop and Edward Dykes the dentist, was the door of the Lauriston Home "for Maternity Rescue Work".

Dr. James Haig Ferguson had founded the Home in 1899. Its rule was plain. It took unmarried girls having their first child, "of otherwise good character", "both before and after their confinement", for five shillings a week, and tried afterward to find them respectable work. Its matron was Miss Murrell. Its twelve places were always full. In the year that ended two weeks after Agnes's son was born, seventy-one girls passed through it. Forty-five of them were domestic servants.

The Home's own case records have not been found. Whether Agnes Brown spent her last weeks there is not known. She was the kind of young woman it was founded for.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: Born at Nine O'Clock
chapters.html:
At nine o'clock on a summer evening, in a hospital that took in women who had nowhere else to go, a servant from the country gave birth to a son.

The Royal Maternity Hospital had been built in 1879 as a memorial to Sir James Young Simpson, the Edinburgh physician who first used chloroform to ease childbirth. The architects, MacGibbon and Ross, had given it the look of a seventeenth-century Scottish town house: two stories over a basement, squared sandstone on the street front, crow-stepped gables, a square corner tower with a conical roof, a round-arched door under a hood molding, and iron railings along the area. A pavilion for married women had been added in 1895, and unmarried women were nursed apart from them.

To be born in 1907 was to be born into a dangerous world. In Scotland more than one baby in nine died before its first birthday. Diarrhea, measles, whooping cough and pneumonia killed children in their thousands every year, and the infants of unmarried mothers, who were often put out to nurse or boarded with strangers, died at nearly twice the rate of others. There were no antibiotics. Smallpox vaccination, required by law for every infant, was the only immunization most families would ever meet; vaccines against typhoid and a few other diseases existed, but none was given to babies, and there was nothing to protect a child from measles, whooping cough or diphtheria. There was no national health service; a doctor cost money that a servant did not have, and a hospital bed was charity.

The Royal Maternity Hospital was one of the places where that was beginning to change. Its wards were a teaching ground for the medical students of the university, and one of its physicians, Dr. John William Ballantyne, was campaigning for something almost nobody yet offered: care for mothers before their babies were born.

In 1907 the hospital was crowded. It delivered about 425 women a year in its own wards, more than one a day, and sent its doctors and pupil midwives out to nearly six hundred more in their homes. Its matron was Miss Edward. Four physicians took charge in turn, a quarter of the year each, among them Professor Sir John Halliday Croom and Dr. Freeland Barbour. Most ordinary deliveries were done by the house surgeons, the students and the pupil midwives. A Biblewoman visited the wards. So did a Ladies' Committee. Most of the women in the beds were servants, farm workers and shop girls.

The city outside was loud and smelled of industry. The cable trams ran up Lauriston Place from Tollcross with the endless hum of the cable in its slot under the street. A few hundred yards to the west, at Fountainbridge, stood the North British Rubber Company's works, the largest factory in Edinburgh, and McEwan's brewery. On a westerly breeze the smell of hot malt and rubber came over the Meadows.

Friday, June 14, 1907, was a mild, dull day. At eight in the morning the air at Leith was still and cloudy, fifty-two degrees, the barometer rising. By six in the evening the Leith station recorded fifty-nine degrees under an overcast sky, with the faintest westerly air. Britain did not yet keep summer time, and in Edinburgh the sun set at about nine.

At nine o'clock that evening, Agnes Brown gave birth to a son.

Overnight the drizzle came on. By the next morning the wind at Leith had gone round to the south-southeast and rain was falling. Mothers were usually kept about ten days. The week that followed was cool and showery for midsummer, barely reaching sixty degrees.

Less than nine years later, a German airship would drop its bombs on Lauriston Place.

Twelve days after the birth, on June 26, 1907, and more than four thousand miles away, a girl was born at Bareilly, in the United Provinces of British India. Her father was Richard Harrison, a colour sergeant in the 1st Battalion, Royal Scots Fusiliers. She was named Helen Ena. Twenty-three years later, in Chicago, she would marry the boy born in Lauriston Place.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: Lawrence Brown, Illegitimate
chapters.html:
She had twenty-one days to register him. She did it on the twentieth.

Scotland had kept civil registers of births, marriages and deaths since 1855, earlier and more thoroughly than most countries. Every birth was entered in a bound register, with the date, the hour, the place, the parents' names and the father's occupation, and a copy went to the Registrar General in Edinburgh. The law was precise about illegitimate children. Under the Registration Act of 1854, the registrar could enter the father of an illegitimate child only if the father and mother asked for it together and both signed the register, or, under later amendments, if a court had found him to be the father. Otherwise the father's column stayed blank, and the word "illegitimate" was written beside the child's name.

For the child, the consequences were real. An illegitimate son had no legal claim on his father, could not inherit from him without a will, and in law belonged to his mother alone. A father could be sued in the sheriff court for aliment, a weekly sum toward the child's keep, but only if the mother could prove who he was and had the money and the nerve to bring the case.

On Thursday, July 4, 1907, the twentieth day, Agnes Brown registered her son at the office of the registrar for the district of St Giles, at 24 Forrest Road. At Leith it was a raw, gray day for July: fifty degrees at eight in the morning, a steady east-northeast breeze off the sea, overcast, with passing showers. The Leith station recorded less than an hour and a half of sunshine all day.

The registrar was R. D. Robertson. He wrote the entry on page 280 of his register, number 839, in the middle of the page.

Name: Lawrence Brown. Born 1907, June fourteenth, 9 h. 0 m. p.m., Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh. Sex: M. Under the name, in brackets, the word the law required: Illegitimate. In the column for the father's name and occupation there was nothing at all. Below it: Agnes Brown, Domestic Servant (domicile Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar). Informant: Agnes Brown, Mother. Registered 1907, July 4th, at Edinburgh. R. D. Robertson, Registrar.

The blank column records what the law allowed that day. The father had not come to the office with her, and no court had named him. Nothing was added to the entry afterward: no court decree, no correction in the margin, no later note. The register tells us nothing more about him, and nothing about whom Agnes told.

The entries on either side of hers were also made for unmarried mothers who registered their children themselves. The one above, made the day before, was for a girl born on June 17 in Drummond Street to Margaret Flynn, a laundress. The one below, made the same day as hers, was for a girl born on June 20 in the same hospital to Barbara Bisset Sherra, a domestic servant, whose domicile was entered as "none fixed." All three children were marked illegitimate.

The name she gave him was not her own father's. Her father had been George. She gave her son the same first name as her uncle, Lawrence Tweedie Brown, her father's elder brother; in the family it was understood that he was named for him.

For her domicile she did not give Lime Tree, the cottage where the census had found her in 1901. She was living at Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

She signed the register as his mother, Agnes Brown, and registered him as Lawrence Brown.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 10
chapters.title: Gean Cottage
chapters.html:
On July 4, 1907, three weeks after her son was born, Agnes Brown gave the registrar in Edinburgh her home address: Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

She did not give Lime Tree Cottage, the house where she had grown up and where her uncle was head of the household. She was living a few doors along the same row. To understand why, you have to know whose house it was.

In 1891 the census enumerator called the row of cottages below Shieldhill "Castle." Later its houses took the names of trees, among them Gean Tree and Lime Tree.

When Agnes came to her grandmother's cottage in the row in 1891, at five, the Archibalds lived a few doors along: the widow Ann Archibald; her daughter Mary, twenty-seven; and her sons Alexander, who broke stones for the roads, and John, who died that June at eighteen (Chapter 3). Mary Archibald was among the first grown women Agnes knew outside her own family.

The 1890s took the Archibald house apart. On December 10, 1897, Ann Archibald died; her name is cut on the family stone. That left Mary in the cottage. And at about the same time, Mary Archibald had a child of her own.

Her gravestone, raised many years later at Biggar, records a daughter, Annie P. R., who died on November 22, 1992, at the age of ninety-four. Annie was born, then, about 1897 or 1898. The man Mary later married, John Cuthbertson, is named on the same stone as "Father." No record yet found shows that Mary was married when her daughter was born. If she was not, then ten years before Agnes, in the same row of cottages, the woman a few doors along had faced the very thing Agnes would face.

On census night in 1901 Mary Archibald, a sewing mistress, was living alone at Gean Tree. Her daughter, about three, was not with her. Her brother Alexander, the stonebreaker of 1891, was now the domestic gardener at Shieldhill House, up the hill. A few doors along, at Lime Tree, Agnes, fifteen, lived with her uncle Andrew, her sister, Mary Brown, and James Parker (Chapter 4). Her grandmother was dead and her aunt Jane had gone. There was no grown woman under that roof.

So who was there to be a mother to her? Not the men at Lime Tree. The grown woman in that row who had known Agnes since she was five, who had buried a brother and a mother of her own, who taught needlework and had a child of her own living elsewhere, was Mary Archibald.

Then the records go quiet for five years.

In the autumn of 1906 Agnes, twenty, conceived a child. On June 14, 1907, her son was born in Edinburgh, and on July 4 she registered him, with the column for his father's name left empty. Her home, she told the registrar, was Gean Cottage.

In 1901 Agnes was living at Lime Tree with her uncle, her sister and James Parker, and Mary Archibald had her own household at Gean Tree. Six years later, when the Edinburgh registrar asked Agnes where she lived, the answer had changed. Those two addresses are why Mary matters to me.

That address is the one piece of the story that survives in Agnes's own words. It does not tell us when Agnes moved in, how long she stayed, or whether Mary went with her to the hospital. Robert and Elizabeth Douglas enter the boy's story later. By the time we see him with them in Edinburgh, he is three.

The record lays it out. Her father, George Brown, died at Edston in April 1886, when she was three and a half months old. Her mother, Christina, died at Quothquan in February 1891, and her grandmother, Jane Henderson, died that June. Agnes was raised in her grandmother's cottage in the row, the house later called Lime Tree, and she was still living there with her uncle Andrew at fifteen, on census night in 1901. When her son was born in the summer of 1907, she was living a few doors along the same row, at Gean Cottage. She said so herself, in the register.

The family records

  • Agnes McGarth Brown born at Edston, Peebles, December 18, 1885: birth register, Peebles 768/00 0149. Open the document
  • Her father, George Brown, died at Edston, April 5, 1886: death register, Peebles. About the death registers (ScotlandsPeople)
  • Her mother, Christina Brown, died at Quothquan, February 10, 1891: Henderson family monument.
  • Her grandmother, Jane Henderson, died June 8, 1891: Quothquan monumental inscriptions.
  • April 5, 1891: Agnes, five, and her sister Mary, seven, in their grandmother Jane Henderson's cottage in the "Castle" row, Libberton; the Archibalds a few doors along: 1891 census, Libberton. Open the census entries
  • March 31, 1901: Agnes, fifteen, niece, at Lime Tree Cottage with her uncle Andrew Henderson (schedule 15); Gean Tree Cottages at schedules 13 and 14: 1901 census, Libberton, ED 3. Open the census entries
  • July 4, 1907: her son's birth registered; mother Agnes Brown, domestic servant, domicile Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar: birth register, St Giles, Edinburgh, 685/04 0839. Open the document

And I believe she did not leave that house the day her son was born. A girl in her position was not simply put out on the road with a newborn. Until the Douglases took him, I think some part of Laurence's first years was spent at Gean Cottage, with his mother and with Mary Archibald, the woman who had become something like a mother to her. Then Agnes did what Mary had done before her. In 1901 Mary Archibald's own daughter, three years old, was living somewhere else. Agnes found her son another home.

Gean Tree Cottage still stands on the Shieldhill Road at Quothquan. On today's map it lies about two hundred feet from the house now called Lime Tree Cottage, though the properties have changed since 1901, and the two cottages of Agnes's girlhood may have stood closer still. In the twentieth century the two small houses were made into one. In 1901 Gean Tree held two households, at schedules 13 and 14, so the address alone does not say which of them took Agnes in.

What she and her brother, the gardener at the big house on the hill, did for Agnes is the subject of the next chapter.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 11
chapters.title: The Gardener and His Sister
chapters.html:
My mother always said a gardener took him in. She was right, and the gardener's sister did the rest.

My mother, Constance Anderson Douglas, told it the same way all her life: a gardener took her father in. She did not know the gardener's name. She had never seen the census of Quothquan, or the birth entry with its address on it. But when I went looking for him, the records led me to one man: Alexander Archibald, the gardener of Shieldhill.

He first comes into view in April 1891, in the row of cottages the village called Castle. He was twenty, the son of a widow, Ann Archibald, born Ann Purves, and the brother of Mary and John. He broke stones for the county roads, hard and poorly paid work out in all weathers. That spring a little girl of five, Agnes Brown, came to live in her grandmother's cottage a few doors along, because her mother had died in February.

The two households grieved together that year. On June 8 Agnes's grandmother, Jane Henderson, died. Twelve days later the Archibalds buried Alexander's brother John, who was eighteen. Within a few weeks, in the same short row of cottages, a five-year-old girl had lost the woman who had taken her in, and a young stonebreaker had lost his brother.

More trouble came to the Archibalds before the decade was out. In December 1897 Alexander's mother died. At about the same time his sister Mary had a daughter of her own, Annie, and no record yet found shows that Mary was married when the child was born. In 1901 Annie was not living with her. So by the end of the 1890s Alexander Archibald knew at first hand what a village said about a child born outside marriage, and what a family did to keep that child safe.

In 1898 Nathaniel Dunlop, the Glasgow shipowner, bought Shieldhill. Within three years the stonebreaker of the Castle row had become the domestic gardener at the big house. On census night in 1901 the laird was away at his house in Govan, and the household living in Shieldhill House was the gardener's: Alexander Archibald, thirty, his wife, Annie, twenty-six, and a dairymaid, Susan Cumisky. Annie had been born at Carnwath, the same parish as Agnes's grandmother.

A domestic gardener kept the grounds of the house and grew the fruit, vegetables and flowers for the family's table. On a place like Shieldhill, where the laird was often in Glasgow and his daughter, Ellen, took a close interest in the running of the estate, the gardener and his wife were among the people who kept the house going from day to day. He knew every servant who came and went, and every servant knew him. Down the hill at Lime Tree, a few doors from his sister's cottage, Agnes Brown was fifteen and about to go into service herself. By 1907 she called herself a domestic servant.

Here is what I believe, and I want to be clear that it is my reading of the record, not the record itself. The register does not say where Agnes worked, but Shieldhill House was the great house of her own village, the likeliest place for a girl from the row to find a place, and Alexander Archibald, a man she had known since she was five, was its gardener. If she was in service there, she worked beside him.

In the autumn of 1906 she found she was carrying a child. She had no father, no mother and no grandmother living, and the house she had grown up in, her uncle's house at Lime Tree, was a house of men. The gardener was the one who could do something about it. He could not keep a pregnant servant in the big house, and he could not take her into his own home on the estate without the whole village asking why. What he could do was send her to his sister.

Mary Archibald lived alone at Gean Tree, a few doors from Lime Tree. She earned her own living with her needle. And she had been through the very thing Agnes was facing: a daughter born before any marriage the records show, raised by someone else. So Agnes left her family home. At Lime Tree she had shared the family home with her sister, Mary Brown, and two single men, her uncle Andrew Henderson and the boarder, James Parker; there was no grown woman in that house to help her. She moved a few doors along, into Gean Cottage, with Mary Archibald, a woman she had known her entire life, who took her in to see her through. That is why, when she registered her son three weeks after his birth, the home she gave the registrar was not her uncle's house but Gean Cottage.

Mary did far more than give her a bed. Through the winter of 1906 and into the spring of 1907, while the child grew, Mary Archibald kept her. A servant found to be pregnant could lose her place at the term, and with it her wages and her board. At Gean Cottage Agnes had a roof, a fire and food on the table when she could no longer earn them. Mary had carried a child herself with no husband beside her, and she knew what lay ahead: the months of hiding it, the talk at the kirk door, the question of where the baby would be born and what would become of him. She was the one who could tell Agnes what to expect, sit with her through the sickness and the waiting, and help her make ready, with her own needle, the things a baby would need. When the time drew near, it was from Mary's house that Agnes set out for Edinburgh. And when she stood before the registrar three weeks after the birth and was asked for her home, it was Mary's house she named.

That is what taking him in meant. The gardener found the place, and his sister kept it. When Agnes came back from Edinburgh with her baby, there was a house in the row with a woman in it who would give them both a loving home, and a man at the big house who had made sure of it. No paper records the arrangement, and I would not expect one; it was the kind of thing a village did quietly. But it fits every record I have found.

In the version of the story that came down to my mother, the gardener's name was Douglas. I think she was joining two true stories into one. A gardener took him in when he was born. A family named Douglas raised him. Over years of retelling, the two were folded together, and the gardener took the family's name. There was even a young Douglas working on the estate in 1901 (Chapter 13).

Some of this can still be tested. No record yet found says whether Alexander was still the gardener at Shieldhill in the autumn of 1906, or where he and Annie were living then. The valuation rolls of Libberton parish for 1905 to 1908 would show who paid the rent on Gean Cottage and on the gardener's house. The estate's wage books, if they survive, would show who worked at Shieldhill House. And the Royal Maternity Hospital's register of births would show where Agnes said she had come from, and where she meant to take her son.

Until those are opened, this is the story as the records and my mother tell it together. A gardener took him in. He did it the only way a working man on someone else's estate could: he sent the girl to his sister, and his sister opened her door. That, to me, was the kindness at the heart of my mother's story. Alexander took Agnes to his sister. Mary took her in.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 12
chapters.title: James Parker
chapters.html:
There was one man who lived under the same roof as Agnes Brown for as long as the records can see her childhood. His name was James Parker.

He first appears in the spring of 1881, in Jane Henderson's cottage at Libberton, a boy of eight. The enumerator wrote down what he was to the family in two words: "Adopted Son." He was not a Henderson. He had been born at Biggar, a few miles down the road, and until his marriage no record says who his parents were, and none says how he came to Jane Henderson's door. He grew up beside her children, Jane, David and little Andrew, and beside her daughter Christina, who would become Agnes's mother.

Ten years later, in April 1891, he was still there. Jane Henderson's house was now in the row called Castle. James was eighteen, an agricultural laborer, and the enumerator wrote "Adopted" again. That was the year Agnes, five, and her sister came to the house (Chapter 3). So from the time Agnes could remember anything, James Parker was part of the house. He was thirteen years older than she was, the boy her grandmother had raised, something between an uncle and an older brother.

In March 1901 the census found him there once more: twenty-eight, a gamekeeper, boarding at Lime Tree Cottage with Andrew Henderson and his two nieces (Chapter 4).

He was no longer the adopted son. He was a lodger who paid his way, a grown man with a trade. The record does not say whose game he kept. The country around Quothquan was a country of estates and shoots. In the same census Robert Arthur was keeper at Huntfield Lodge and Robert Clarkson at Cormiston. Shieldhill, the big house above the village, had been bought three years before by a Glasgow shipowner. A keeper's work was out of doors and at all hours: rearing birds in the spring, walking the moor and the woods, beating for the guns from the twelfth of August into the winter. Lime Tree was a short walk from all of it.

He was not the only grown man under that roof. The head of the house was Agnes's uncle, Andrew Henderson, her mother's younger brother. He had been a boy of five in the cottage in 1881 and fourteen in 1891, when Agnes came to it. By 1901 he was twenty-five, a groom who worked with horses, and the man whose name stood first on the census page. Agnes depended on him for the roof over her head.

So in 1901 the house where Agnes was growing up held two men who were not her father: her uncle, who was its head, and James Parker, who boarded there. No record says anything about either man's conduct toward her, and this book does not suggest it. But a family history that asks who the father was cannot leave out the men she lived with.

Three censuses, twenty years, and the same household each time. In a village where people came and went at every term day, James Parker stayed.

He went on staying. In 1911 the census found him again, ten years older and still on the estate.

On census night, Sunday, April 2, 1911, James Parker was living at 3 Shieldhill Mains, on the estate itself, in a house of three rooms. He was thirty-eight, a gamekeeper still, born at Biggar. He was the head of his own household now. With him were his wife, Janet, thirty-four, born at Dunoon in Argyll, and their three children, all born in the parish: John, five; Euphemia, three; and Robert, one. Janet told the enumerator that she had been married seven years.

So he had not left. On August 28, 1903, at Coldstream, in the parish of Carluke, he married Janet Crawford Stewart, a domestic servant of twenty-four and a shepherd's daughter, by the forms of the United Free Church. He signed his full name: James Lawson Parker. He gave his trade as gamekeeper and his home as Shieldhill, Biggar. That was three years before my grandfather was conceived.

The marriage entry also answered the oldest question about him. For his father he named Benjamin Parker, a mason, deceased. For his mother he named Jane Lawson, a lady's maid, deceased. She is entered under her own name alone. A boy called James Lawson was registered at Biggar in 1872, the year James Parker was born, with no mother's maiden surname in the index, which is how the registers usually show a child whose mother was not married. That birth entry has not been opened. But it is likely that the "adopted son" of Jane Henderson's cottage began life as James Lawson, the child of a servant, and took his father's name later.

If so, Agnes grew up beside a boy whose start in life was the one her own son would have: a servant's child, raised by another family, under a name that was not on his birth record.

He brought his wife home to Shieldhill. In the autumn of 1906, when Agnes conceived, he was a married man of thirty-three with a baby son, keeping game on the estate where she lived and, I believe, worked. My mother said the father was on the grounds. James Parker was on the grounds.

That cuts two ways, and I want to be fair to both. A man with a wife and an infant at home could not have married a pregnant girl of twenty, and a household like his had every reason to keep quiet. That would explain the silence that came down to my mother. But a wife and a new baby are also reasons to think he had a life of his own, a few doors from Agnes's, that had nothing to do with hers. The census cannot tell us which. It only takes away the easy story that he vanished.

The same page tells one more thing. At Gean Tree Cottage in 1911 lived Andrew Rodger, a farmer of sixty-five, and his wife, Jane. Mary Archibald was gone from the house where Agnes had said she lived.

The man who had shared a roof with Agnes longer than anyone outside her own blood was still a near neighbor in 1906, the year that matters most.

There is one more voice to set beside the census. My mother said that Agnes lived on the Shieldhill estate with the man who fathered her son. She remembered him as someone important there and thought he might have been a doctor. She believed his position was why so little had come down to her. She was sure of something else about her father's early life: a gardener named Douglas took him in. It was I who wondered whether the man she remembered as a doctor might have been Nathaniel Dunlop.

The most important man at Shieldhill was its owner. Nathaniel Dunlop had been born at Campbeltown on April 7, 1830, so in the autumn of 1906 he was seventy-six, a widower of almost forty years with one grown daughter, Ellen. On June 28, 1907, when Laurence was two weeks old, his name was in the birthday honours, reported as far away as Canada. On July 15 he was knighted at Buckingham Palace. My mother thought the man might have been a doctor. What she remembered most clearly was his importance at the estate. Years later I came across a line printed while my grandfather was still a little boy: "Sir Nathaniel Dunlop, LL.D., of Shieldhill, Biggar." Dunlop was a shipowner. Glasgow had made him an honorary Doctor of Laws. I wondered then what the word "doctor" had meant to the person who first told her.

Agnes named a cottage at Shieldhill as her home. Nathaniel Dunlop owned the estate. Counting back the usual nine months from June 14, 1907, brings you to about the third week of September 1906. What I still wanted to know was whose house she worked in that autumn, the autumn before my grandfather was born.

I think Agnes worked at Shieldhill House. She was a domestic servant, the house was close to home, and Mary Archibald's brother had worked there as a gardener. If I wanted to know where a young woman from that row might have found a place, I would start with Alexander and the house where he tended the grounds. Whether Dunlop fathered Laurence is a further question.

The question can be answered. The birth entry of James Lawson, Biggar, 1872, would show whether a father was named and where Jane Lawson was in service. The Royal Maternity Hospital's register of births for those years survives, and it asked every mother for her last and her future place of residence: where Agnes said she had come from, and where she meant to go with her son. A Lanark Sheriff Court action for aliment, the Scots term for maintenance, might have named the father; no matching action appears in the published index consulted for 1907 births. An estate wage book would show whose keeper he was. And there is DNA. If Laurence's descendants match people named Parker or Lawson, or with roots in Biggar, and those matches connect through none of Agnes's own families, the record will have spoken.

Until then, James Parker stands where the census left him in 1911: a gamekeeper of thirty-eight, with a wife and three children, at Shieldhill Mains, on the same estate as Gean Cottage.

chapters.label: Chapter 13
chapters.title: Lochrin Place
chapters.html:
After the fourth of July, 1907, the boy disappears from the record.

No paper tells us when Agnes Brown and her son were parted, or how, or who made the arrangement. Agnes's home was Gean Cottage, and he may have spent his first months there, perhaps longer, before he went to the Douglases. The records cannot yet say.

There is one name that may yet bridge the two worlds, and it is the name he grew up with. On census night in 1901, in the estate row at Shieldhill, a few houses from Gean Tree, a young joiner was boarding with the estate's grieve. He was twenty, born at Cargill in Perthshire, and his name was Donald Douglas. A Douglas was working on the estate where Agnes lived, and the boy she gave birth to was raised by a family named Douglas. My mother's memory of a gardener named Douglas is told in Chapter 11. Donald had been born at Cargill on May 5, 1880, the son of Kenneth Douglas, a railway surfaceman, and Janet Buchan. Robert Douglas, the stone machineman in Edinburgh who would raise Laurence, was the son of Archibald Douglas, a forester, and Isabella Gray. They were not brothers. Whether their fathers were kin, no record yet says, and no record links Donald to the boy's placement. How Laurence came from Agnes Brown's care into the home of Robert and Lizzie Douglas remains unknown.

If Donald Douglas turns out to belong to the same family as Robert, two possibilities open, and I cannot help wondering about both. He may have been the one who found the boy a permanent home among his own people. Or he may have been the father, a young man who could not or would not marry, letting his own kin take his son. Either would explain how a child from a cottage row in Clydesdale came to be raised by a stone machineman's family in Edinburgh and Fife. Neither can be tested until the records show whether Kenneth and Archibald Douglas were brothers or cousins.

Look at Quothquan on a map and you see how small Agnes's world was: a few dozen houses under a hill, the big house at the top of the road, fields on every side, and Biggar four miles off. A servant girl had no car and no telephone, and she worked six days of the week. The railway at Thankerton was a mile and a half away, but a girl in service did not go far or often. I believe the father was a man she saw every day, on the estate itself, which is what my mother was told.

Put the pieces side by side and they tell one story, the way a small village of working people would have handled a thing like this. A young servant girl on the estate is with child, and the father, as my mother was told, is someone important there, someone whose name could not be spoken. She is not sent to the poorhouse. She is taken in. The gardener of the big house is the brother of the woman a few doors along, and when Agnes gives her home address after the birth, it is Gean Cottage, the house where Mary Archibald lived. Mary had once had a child of her own who was raised by someone else. Then, quietly, the boy is found a permanent home far from Quothquan, with a family named Douglas, and a Douglas had worked on that same estate. By the spring of 1911, when he was not yet four, he was Laurence B. Douglas, the son of the house in an Edinburgh tenement. I think two decisions have come down to us as one: where Agnes could take her newborn that summer, and who would raise him. There was time between them for my grandfather to have lived with his mother.

That is my reading. Every piece of it rests on a record or on my mother's memory, but the thread that ties them together is mine, and the records that could prove or break it are still waiting in the archives. There is no court order, no receipt, no letter. She was twenty-one, a servant with no husband and no money. She would marry, have daughters, and go on with her own life. If she ever wrote down what she felt about the son who grew up under another family's name, it has not come down to us.

Those were the years in which the British state first began to take responsibility for its poorest children. The Children Act of 1908 strengthened the laws against neglecting a child, set up juvenile courts, and forbade children to be sold drink or tobacco. In Scotland, the parish councils had long boarded out orphans and deserted children with families in the country, paying a few shillings a week for their keep, and thousands of Edinburgh and Glasgow children grew up that way in Highland and Borders villages. Others were taken in privately by relatives, neighbors or couples who wanted a child, with no paperwork at all.

For nearly four years no record that has come to light places him anywhere. There is no baptism, no poor-law entry, no court paper, no letter. When he surfaces again, on census night, Sunday, April 2, 1911, he has another family and another name.

The enumerator found him at 16 Lochrin Place, at Tollcross in Edinburgh, about half a mile from the hospital in Lauriston Place where he had been born. The page lists no head of the house. Elizabeth Douglas, thirty-six, gave herself as the wife, born at Gilmerton in Midlothian. Below her came Janet, ten, a schoolgirl, born in Edinburgh. Then came Laurence B. Douglas, three, son, born in Edinburgh. A boarder, Donald Steven, twenty-five, a tailor from Caithness, made up the household.

The census did not ask whether a child was adopted, nursed or boarded out. It asked his relation to the head of the family, and the answer was son. At three he was already living under the Douglas name, and he carried a middle initial, B, almost certainly for Brown, the name he was born with. It is the earliest record yet found that calls him Douglas, and it spells his first name the way he would spell it as a man.

The census asked every married woman how many children had been born alive to the present marriage, and how many were still living. Elizabeth had been married eleven years. She answered two and two. On this census page there were two children, Janet and Laurence. The columns do not name the children she counted.

The family was still in Edinburgh in the spring of 1911. Within sixteen months it had moved to Dunfermline.

How a baby born at Lauriston Place to a servant from Clydesdale came, by the age of three or four, to be living as the son of a stone machineman and his wife is the largest silence in his life.

What can be said is this. Lizzie Douglas had begun her own life in his position: born to an unmarried servant, no father on the record, left behind when her mother married and sailed for New Zealand, and raised by others. The family remembered that she and Robert had lost an infant daughter, Isabella, sometime after 1900, though Elizabeth's census answer of 1911 does not settle the matter either way. A woman who had been taken in took in a child.

There was a law that could have left a trace. Under Part I of the Children Act of 1908, in force from 1909, anyone who took a child under seven to nurse for payment had to notify the local authority, and in Scotland the parish councils kept registers of such guardians. If the Douglases were paid to keep him, the arrangement should have been reported. No such notice for him has been found.

In those same years, his mother's life went on without him.

chapters.label: Chapter 14
chapters.title: Nurse Brown of the Asylum
chapters.html:
She went to work as a nurse in an asylum. In 1911 she married a man who worked there.

By the summer of 1911 Agnes Brown was a nurse at the Royal Edinburgh Asylum in Morningside.

Asylum nursing was one of the few careers open to a working woman without education or connections. In the 1890s the Medico-Psychological Association had begun examining asylum attendants and awarding a certificate. The Royal Edinburgh Asylum stood on high ground on the south side of the city, a small town of its own. Its main building, West House, was a long, three-story block of sandstone with ivy on its walls. Under its famous physician-superintendent, Sir Thomas Clouston, it had become known for treating its patients as patients rather than prisoners, with work, gardens, entertainment and dances. Clouston retired in 1908. His successor, Dr. George Matthew Robertson, a believer in women nurses, put them onto the men's wards.

The work was hard. Asylum nurses in Scotland in those years commonly worked more than seventy hours a week, lived in, needed leave to go out, and earned around sixteen pounds a year with board in their first years. They were expected to bring "a good moral character". They wore uniform, a long cotton dress, a starched white apron and a white cap, with keys at the belt. In return the work gave training, a bed and a future: the Association's certificate, examined twice a year inside the asylums, could take a woman to charge nurse. When a nurse married, she was often expected to leave.

On Monday, August 28, 1911, Agnes married at 34 Chambers Street in the Old Town. It was not a church wedding. It was a marriage by declaration, a legal Scottish form: the couple declared themselves married before two witnesses, and a sheriff's warrant allowed the registrar to record it. By the late 1930s about one Scottish marriage in eight would be made that way.

The entry, on page 308 of the register for St Giles, number 616, records the groom as Thomas McKay McKenzie, asylum attendant, bachelor, aged twenty-one, of West House, Royal Asylum, Morningside, Edinburgh. His father was John Alexander McKenzie, coastguardsman. His mother, Mary McKenzie, maiden surname McKay, was dead. The bride signed as Agnes McGarth Brown, asylum nurse, spinster, aged twenty-five, of the same place. Her father was George Brown, farm grieve, deceased. Her mother, Christina Brown, maiden surname Henderson, deceased. The witnesses were Edward Thomson, asylum attendant, and John McIntyre, coachman. The warrant of the sheriff-substitute of the Lothians and Peebles was dated the same day. The registrar was R. D. Robertson, the same man who had written down her son's birth four years before.

Agnes was four years older than her husband. In the column for her condition the record says spinster, which was true: she had never been married.

At ten in the morning on May 6, 1912, at 9 Stewart Terrace, Edinburgh, she gave birth to a daughter. Mary Christina McKenzie was registered at Morningside, number 456, page 152. Her father was still an asylum attendant.

In August 1914, the month the war began, a second daughter was born in Edinburgh: Jean Henderson McKenzie, who carried the surname of Agnes's mother's people.

The war changed the asylums as it changed everything else. By the end of 1914 the Royal Edinburgh Asylum had lost many of its male attendants to the army, and women took their places on the wards. In January 1916 Parliament passed conscription for single men, and that spring for married men too.

On December 9, 1915, Thomas McKenzie attested for the army. He gave his work as barman. On his family form he listed his wife, Agnes McKenzie, of 62 Balcarres Street, Edinburgh, and his two daughters: Mary, born May 6, 1912, and Jean, born August 1914. Later someone crossed out the Balcarres Street address and wrote instead, care of G. Thomson, Sherwood, Bonnyrigg, Midlothian. Thomas served at home from 1916 to 1919.

There was no son on the form. The boy was in Fife by then, with another family and another name.

On opposite shores of the Firth of Forth, a mother was raising two little girls, and the boy she had borne was growing up as someone else's son.

chapters.label: Chapter 15
chapters.title: A New Family, a New Name
chapters.html:
In 1912 the family that had taken him in left Edinburgh, and the boy went with them, across the Forth to a new town.

By the summer of 1912 the Douglases had crossed the Firth of Forth to Dunfermline. They took a flat at 36 Victoria Terrace, a long street of sandstone tenements, four stories high, with bay windows and tall chimneys.

Dunfermline was a good town to move to in 1912. It was the old royal burgh of Fife, where Robert the Bruce and other Scottish kings are buried in the abbey, a town of linen mills and coal pits on the hill above the estuary, and the birthplace of Andrew Carnegie, the weaver's son who had become one of the richest men in the world. Carnegie had given the town a public library, swimming baths, and Pittencrieff Park and Glen, and his Carnegie Dunfermline Trust was charged with bringing into the lives of the town's working people "more of sweetness and light." The linen mills still wove fine damask table linen for hotels and ocean liners. And three miles to the south, on the shore of the Forth, the Admiralty had begun in 1909 to build a great new naval dockyard at Rosyth, to face the German fleet across the North Sea. Thousands of men were coming to work on it, and the town was growing.

On Monday, August 19, 1912, the boy was admitted to the Queen Anne School.

The Queen Anne School stood in the middle of the town, a tall Victorian building with stepped gables, its infants' department on one side of the yard and the older children's on the other. The clerk opened the infant admission register and wrote the boy in.

Name: Lawrence Douglas. Date of birth: June 14, 1907. Name of parent or guardian: Robert Douglas. Address: 36 Victoria Terrace. Previous school: None. In the column for the child's relationship to the guardian, the clerk wrote one word.

Adopted.

The boy was five years, two months and five days old. Five years after a registrar in Edinburgh wrote Lawrence Brown, a school clerk in Dunfermline wrote Lawrence Douglas.

The word did not mean what it would mean later. Scotland had no legal adoption until the Adoption of Children (Scotland) Act of 1930. In 1912 "adopted" meant that a family had taken a child in and was raising him as its own. It described a household, not a court order. The register does not say who the boy's natural parents were.

Two days later, on Wednesday, August 21, the same school admitted Janet Douglas, twelve, to its primary department. She had come from the Commercial School. Her entry gave the same address and the same guardian. The two entries put the girl of twelve and the boy of five in the same house and the same school, the daughter born to Robert and Lizzie Douglas and the boy they had taken in.

chapters.label: Chapter 16
chapters.title: A Boy in Dunfermline
chapters.html:
He grew up three miles from the new naval dockyard at Rosyth, in the years when the battlecruisers of the Royal Navy sailed to war from the Firth of Forth.

In August 1914, when Britain went to war, Laurence was seven and Janet fourteen. On August 1 she had left school, because she had reached the age at which she could. In Edinburgh that same month his mother, Agnes, gave birth to his second half-sister, Jean. No record I have found names the two of them together.

In December 1914 Admiral Beatty's battlecruisers came to anchor in the Forth off Rosyth, and for four years the town lived beside the war. Sailors filled the streets on shore leave. Searchlights swept the sky over the Firth at night. Schoolchildren collected for the troops, knitted socks and wrote letters to men at the front.

On Tuesday, January 11, 1916, he was moved up from the infants into Queen Anne Primary. The register gives his number as 1191. His guardian was still Robert Douglas. The family had moved. They now lived at 5 Foundry Street, Dunfermline.

On the evening of May 30, 1916, Beatty's battlecruisers sailed out of the Forth to meet the German fleet off Jutland, in the greatest naval battle of the war. More than six thousand British sailors were killed, and on June 2 the damaged ships came back up the Firth to Rosyth, carrying their wounded.

Laurence loved to read, all his life, and Dunfermline was a good town for a boy who loved books. In 1883 Andrew Carnegie had given his birthplace the first of the public libraries he would go on to build in more than two thousand towns around the world, and over its door were carved the words "Let There Be Light." It stood a short walk up the hill from Foundry Street, its shelves full of Stevenson and Scott and the adventure stories of the day.

In November 1918 the war ended, and ten days after the Armistice the surrendered German High Seas Fleet was brought into the Firth of Forth under escort before being taken north to Scapa Flow. Then came the influenza. In the winter of 1918–19 the pandemic killed more people across the world than the war had, and many thousands in Scotland.

The men came home in 1919, some whole, some on crutches, some with empty sleeves pinned to their jackets, some with lungs burned by gas. Laurence was eleven and twelve in those years. The fathers and big brothers of the boys in his class were among them.

Robert Douglas was not a soldier, and the war did not take him. He had had lupus since he was a boy, the kind of tuberculosis that eats at the skin, and in his last year it had reached his lungs. Tuberculosis was the great killer of working Scotland, and its patients were sent away from their families to sanatoriums for rest and fresh air. Robert was taken to Woodburn Sanatorium, on Canaan Lane in Morningside, on the south side of Edinburgh. He died there at half past seven on the morning of Tuesday, September 9, 1919. He was forty-three. Elizabeth registered the death the same day, giving her address as 5 Foundry Street, Dunfermline, and herself as his widow. The registrar wrote his trade as stone machineman, and his parents as Archibald Douglas, forester, and Isabella Gray.

Laurence was twelve.

On Friday, October 8, 1920, he left school for good. He was thirteen years and almost four months old. The school-leaving age was fourteen. The register gives the reason in four words: "Granted Exemption by E.A." The local education authority had let him go early. Families asked for an exemption when they needed a boy's wages, or when a job had been found for him. The register does not say which. By then the house in Foundry Street had been without a man's wage for more than a year. It does not say what work he went to.

Nine years later, on the passenger list, he described himself as a grocer.

chapters.label: Chapter 17
chapters.title: Zeppelins Over Edinburgh
chapters.html:
On Sunday, April 2, 1916, the war came to the city where Laurence was born.

By the spring of 1916 the war had become a war against civilians as well as soldiers. German submarines were sinking merchant ships without warning, and a year earlier one of them had torpedoed the Lusitania off Ireland with the loss of nearly twelve hundred lives. German airships had been bombing England since January 1915. No bomb had yet fallen on a Scottish city.

He was eight years old that spring, a schoolboy in Dunfermline. In January he had moved up to the primary at Queen Anne School, and the register gave his home as 5 Foundry Street, with Robert Douglas as his guardian. Three miles south of the house, on the north shore of the Firth of Forth, lay the naval dockyard at Rosyth, base of Admiral Beatty's battlecruisers. That night Rosyth and the Forth Bridge were the airships' targets.

Four German naval airships set out across the North Sea that afternoon for the Forth: L13, L14, L16 and L22. Each was more than five hundred feet long and carried a crew of about nineteen. L13 developed engine trouble and turned back. L16 crossed the Northumberland coast and dropped her bombs in open country short of Newcastle.

L22, under Kapitänleutnant Martin Dietrich, crossed the coast north of Berwick-upon-Tweed at about nine o'clock. Dietrich believed he was over the Tyne, and most of his bombs fell harmlessly in the fields near Chirnside in Berwickshire. Later L22 came up toward the Forth. Accounts of what she did there disagree; some have her dropping her last bombs on the southern edge of Edinburgh. The bombs that fell on Leith and on the city itself, as the police and the Burgh Engineer recorded them that night, were the work of a single airship, L14.

L14's commander was Kapitänleutnant Alois Böcker, a former merchant navy captain. He crossed the coast near St. Abb's Head, took his bearing from the Isle of May, and flew up the middle of the Firth.

The warning reached Edinburgh and Leith in the evening. At half past nine the military ordered air-raid action. Electric street lamps were dimmed and the fire brigade, the hospitals and the Red Cross were put on alert. But most of the city's homes were lit by gas, and gas was not cut off, so the people in them had no signal at all. Out in Leith Roads, the ships at anchor kept their lights burning. A naval pilot, Sub-Lieutenant G. A. Cox, took off from East Fortune in an Avro biplane armed with a single machine gun, never found the airship, and was hurt landing in the dark. Rosyth lay blacked out and was not found. Leith was.

At about a quarter past eleven L14 hung over the island of Inchkeith while Böcker took his bearings from the anchored ships. The night was clear, with a low haze. At about 11:25 Leith police saw her, perhaps ten thousand feet up, moving south-southwest toward the docks.
