The first bomb, a 110-pound high explosive, fell into Edinburgh Dock, sank two rowing boats and blew in the skylights of a Danish sailing ship. Two incendiaries near the Albert Dock set a fence on fire. Two more high explosives struck a grain warehouse in the Timberbush and the Custom House quay.

The sixth bomb came through the roof of the tenement at 2 Commercial Street and burst in a top-floor flat. Robert Love, an engineer, was killed in his bed. At number 14, an incendiary set a flat alight, and an elderly woman downstairs put the fire out with a pan of water.

The eleventh bomb hit Innes and Grieve's bonded warehouse on Ronaldson's Wharf. The whisky inside caught fire and lit the sky over Leith. Forty-four thousand pounds' worth of spirit burned. The firm was not insured against attack from the air.

An incendiary fell into a room at 15 Church Street where a mother and her three children lay asleep; it was smothered before anyone was hurt. Four incendiaries gutted the manse of St. Thomas' Church in Mill Lane; the minister, his family and their servant got out unharmed. High explosives burst outside St. Thomas' School and outside Leith Hospital.

In Bonnington, at 200 Bonnington Road, a splinter from one of four bombs killed David Robb, aged one, asleep in his cot. His parents, Robert and Jane Robb, had buried another baby the year before.

At about ten minutes to midnight a bomb blew out windows at the end of Bellevue Terrace. Then Böcker turned south, over the New Town, toward the Old. An incendiary bounced harmlessly on the Mound. The next high-explosive bomb came through the roof of 39 Lauriston Place.

Lauriston Place was the street on which Laurence had been born. The Royal Maternity Hospital stood at number 79, a short way along from the house that was hit. The bomb at number 39 wrecked the roof and part of a wall of Dr. McLaren's house; the doctor, his wife and their teenage daughter climbed out unhurt, and kept a piece of the bomb's nose cap. Next door it damaged the special school for children with ringworm. A fragment of the same bomb struck David Robertson, twenty-seven, a gunner invalided out of the Royal Field Artillery, in the street outside. He died of the wound in hospital.

Another bomb landed in the playground of George Watson's College, beside the Royal Infirmary, and smashed its classrooms. An incendiary fell on the roof of the Infirmary itself: a cone of oil and kerosene wrapped in tarred rope. It did no damage.

The airship swung across the Meadows. A bomb at 82 Marchmont Crescent failed to burst properly and drove down through the floors into the ground-floor flat at number 80. Incendiaries dropped into gardens at 31 Hatton Place, opposite the Sick Children's Hospital, and at 28 Blacket Place. At 183 Causewayside a high explosive practically wrecked a tenement and injured six people. Wilhelmina Henderson, an elderly woman who lived there, died of a heart attack brought on by the shock.

L14 turned back toward the Castle. A bomb exploded in the Grassmarket outside the White Hart Hotel, blew in nearly every window in the square, and wounded four men. One of them, William Breakey, forty-five, a Corporation porter, died of his wound. Another bomb struck the southwest face of the Castle Rock, narrowly missing the fortress. Two more fell near the Water of Leith and blew out the stained-glass windows of the chapel at Donaldson's Hospital.

At about 12:25 a.m., on what was by then Monday, April 3, the deadliest bomb of the night came down in the street outside the tenement at 16 Marshall Street, off Nicolson Square. Men and boys had crowded into the close. Six died there: John Smith, forty-one, and his son William, fifteen; Henry Rumble, seventeen; William Ewing, twenty-three; Victor MacFarlane; and David Graham, five years old. Seven more were wounded, among them another of John Smith's sons and Henry Rumble's father. Private Thomas Donoghue, twenty-four, of the 3/4th Royal Scots, home on leave, was carried away with wounds to the abdomen and became the seventh to die from Marshall Street.

A bomb on Haddon's Court fatally injured James Farquhar, a mason of seventy-three; he died in hospital five days later. Another, outside 69 St. Leonard's Hill, killed Cora Edmond Bell, four, in her bed, and injured her mother and her younger sister.

As the airship passed over the King's Park, soldiers from the rifle range under Salisbury Crags fired at her, and a Vickers machine gun opened up from the park. They did not reach her. The forty-fourth and final bomb fell in the grounds of Prestonfield House at about 12:40. L14 turned east, crossed the coast near Dunbar about one o'clock, and went home across the North Sea.

She had been over Leith and Edinburgh for about an hour and a quarter. She had dropped forty-four bombs, twenty on Leith and twenty-four on the city, and had hit no military target. In Leith and Edinburgh together the official count was thirteen dead and twenty-four injured; reconstructions from the city's police reports, which include those who died of their wounds in the days that followed, name fourteen dead. No other German attack on Scottish soil in the war killed so many civilians.

In December 1915 his mother, Agnes, was living in the city. Her husband, Thomas McKenzie, had given their address to the army as 62 Balcarres Street, Morningside, where Agnes lived with their daughters, Mary, not yet four, and Jean, sixteen months. Six days after the raid, on Saturday, April 8, Thomas reported for army service.

The newspapers were not allowed to say where the bombs had fallen. When the reports appeared on Tuesday, April 4, the censor permitted only "south-east Scottish counties" and "an eastern coastal town." The dead were buried that Wednesday and Thursday. Two babies born in the Southside that spring were named for the night: Catherine O'May Campbell Raida Smith, born on April 2 itself at 49 Montague Street, and Raida Alexandra Douglas, born on May 21 at 88 Nicolson Street.

Afterward the city learned. The gas would now be cut with the electricity when the warning came. An anti-aircraft gun, a searchlight and a listening device were dug in on Corstorphine Hill, and gun pits on Wester Craiglockhart Hill. The Governor of the Castle moved the Honours of Scotland, the crown, scepter and sword, down from the Crown Room into the vaults. Alois Böcker was brought down that September in command of L33 after a raid on London, and taken prisoner. The Marchmont Crescent bomb is on display today at the National Museum of Flight, at East Fortune, the airfield from which the lone pilot had gone up that night.

chapters.label: Chapter 18
chapters.title: The Mother He Claimed
chapters.html:
In the 1920s Lizzie Douglas, the woman who had raised him, becomes Elizabeth Anderson. In every record that names her, Laurence calls her his mother.

The census of Sunday, June 19, 1921, found them still at 5 Foundry Street, in three rooms. Laurence had turned fourteen five days before. Elizabeth Douglas, forty-seven, was the head of the house now, and she gave her condition as widow. She worked as a school cleaner for the Fife Education Authority. Janet, twenty-one, was a clerkess with the Dunfermline Co-operative Society. Lawrence, fourteen, son, born in Edinburgh, had left school and gone to work as a message boy for a grocer, McClelland and Company. It was the start of the trade he would give at the border eight years later: grocer. A boarder, Margaret Dobson, thirty-seven, a saleswoman, helped pay the rent.

For every child under fifteen, the 1921 census asked whether the child's parents were living. Beside Lawrence's name the answer is "F. D.": father dead. Robert Douglas had died at Woodburn Sanatorium in September 1919.

The 1920s were hard years in Fife. After a brief boom at the end of the war, the economy collapsed in 1921, and for the rest of the decade more than a million British workers were unemployed. The linen trade was shrinking. In the middle of the decade the Admiralty reduced Rosyth Dockyard to care and maintenance, and thousands of men in and around Dunfermline lost their work. In May 1926 the General Strike shut down Britain for nine days in support of the coal miners, and when it collapsed the Fife miners stayed locked out for seven months, through the summer and autumn, living on soup kitchens and parish relief.

By 1929 Elizabeth was using the surname Anderson; the passenger lists of that year name her as Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson of 39 Grieve Street, mother of both Laurence and Janet. When and whom she remarried has not yet been found in the records.

Laurence did so again ten years later, applying to marry in Alabama, when he gave his parents' names as Robert Douglas and Elizabeth McDonald. Twenty-two years later his obituary named them as Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. Under each of her names, she was the mother he claimed.

chapters.label: Chapter 19
chapters.title: Janet Sails First
chapters.html:
Janet went first.

They had grown up in the same house, though only she had been born to the parents who raised them. She was seven years older than Laurence, and the school registers in Dunfermline record the two of them in the same household from 1912.

On Friday, July 16, 1926, Janet Douglas married Thomas Crombie in Dunfermline. She was twenty-six. He was thirty-two, a man from Kinross. Years later, in Chicago, each of them would swear to the date and place on a naturalization petition, and their sworn accounts agree. It was the summer of the miners' lockout, with the Fife pits closed and the dockyard at Rosyth idle.

They were part of one of the great migrations in Scottish history. In the 1920s some four hundred thousand people left Scotland, so many that the country's population fell during the decade. Most went to Canada and the United States. America had closed its doors to most of Europe with the Immigration Act of 1924, which set strict quotas by nationality, but the quota for Great Britain was the largest of all, and Scots who could show they would not become a public charge could still get in. Many, like Janet and Thomas, went by way of Canada and crossed the border by train at Detroit or Port Huron.

Within two months they were gone. On September 13, 1926, they crossed into the United States at Detroit. Janet's petition gives the means of travel as "C.P.R.R." Thomas's gives it as "C.P. No. 19". They settled on the West Side of Chicago, on South Kostner Avenue, in a district of two-flats and frame cottages. By 1930 Thomas was selling furniture.

Laurence was nineteen. He stayed behind in Dunfermline with the woman he called his mother. When he next appears in the records, three years later, he is a grocer, and his sister has come home.

chapters.label: Chapter 20
chapters.title: Last Days in Scotland
chapters.html:
Janet came home in the spring of 1929, and when she left again that autumn, she did not leave alone.

On Saturday, May 18, 1929, she landed at Greenock from Quebec aboard the Canadian Pacific liner Montroyal, traveling third class. The passenger list describes her as Janet Crombie, twenty-nine, married, housewife. Her address in Britain would be 39 Grieve Street, Dunfermline, her mother's house. Her permanent residence was the United States, and she intended to go back. She came alone.

Dunfermline in 1929 was a town of gray stone and red pantile roofs climbing a hill above the Forth, with the square tower of the Abbey at the top and the ruined palace of the Scottish kings below it in the glen. Trams ran down to Rosyth and out to the mining villages. Grocers' assistants like Laurence stood behind long counters in white aprons, weighing out sugar and tea into paper bags, slicing bacon and cheese, cutting butter from a block with wooden pats.

There is a photograph of the two of them from the 1920s, and it is the best picture we have of him. No date or place is written on it. Two copies have been shared online by other researchers of the family, who identify the pair as Janet and Laurence.

They are standing against an iron railing in front of a whitewashed wall, on a bright day, and both of them are eating ice-cream cones. Janet, on the left, is small and neat in a long double-breasted coat with big round buttons, her dark hair cut in a short bob with a heavy fringe. She has a cone in each hand, one for herself and one waiting, and she is looking at the camera with a sidelong half-smile.

Laurence is much taller. He leans back against the railing with one long leg crossed in front of the other. His face is long and fine-boned, with a high forehead, a straight nose and a clean-shaven chin. His hair is cut short at the sides and combed straight back from his forehead. His eyes, the blue eyes the immigration inspector would write down, are half closed as he bites into the ice cream. He wears a jacket with a white handkerchief folded in the breast pocket, a V-neck sweater trimmed with a stripe at the neck, a dark tie, a belt, and the wide, high-waisted trousers of the late twenties, pressed to a crease. In the family he was remembered as a man who was always impeccably dressed, his hair perfectly combed. The photograph agrees.

On Tuesday, September 3, 1929, the American consulate at Glasgow issued Laurence an immigration visa. The law required an applicant to produce a birth certificate where one could be had, and his birth certificate said Lawrence Brown. So it was as Lawrence Brown, not Lawrence Douglas, that the United States first knew him.

Four days later, when Janet sailed back to America, her brother sailed with her. He had a ticket, a visa and fifty dollars.

chapters.label: Chapter 21
chapters.title: Six Feet Tall, Fair Hair, Blue Eyes
chapters.html:
He was twenty-two, he had fifty dollars, and he was going to America.

On Saturday, September 7, 1929, they sailed from Greenock on the Duchess of Bedford.

Greenock, at the mouth of the Clyde, was where Glasgow's emigrants had said goodbye for a century. Up the river the cranes and the steel skeletons of ships stood along the water from the Broomielaw down past Govan and Clydebank. The Duchess of Bedford had been built there, at John Brown's yard in Clydebank, one of the Canadian Pacific's new "Duchess" liners for the run from Scotland to the St. Lawrence. The shipbuilders had photographed her interiors the year before. Her A Deck dining saloon was a great octagonal room under a coffered, painted ceiling, with a gallery running round it and tables for four laid with white cloths. Her observation lounge on the promenade deck had patterned carpets, chintz armchairs, a fireplace and tall windows. Her cabins had two or three berths with curtains, a washbasin, a radiator, and a porthole.

The British outward list puts brother and sister on the cabin-class page. Janet's ticket was number 32480. His was 33082. Both gave the same address, 39 Grieve Street. The master was Captain H. Sibbons. The contracted port of landing was Montreal.

On the ship's incoming manifest she is line 3: Janet Crombie, twenty-nine, married, housewife, born in Edinburgh, returning to Chicago. He is line 10: Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, single, grocer, born in Edinburgh, last permanent residence Dunfermline. For his nearest relative in Scotland he wrote: Mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson, 39 Grieve St. For the person he was going to: his brother-in-law, Thomas Crombie, 1534 South Kostner Avenue, Chicago.

A great anticyclone sat over the British Isles that day. The morning forecast for the southwest of Scotland read: "Light or moderate westerly breeze; fair; warm." At Renfrew, outside Glasgow, no rain fell, no sunshine was recorded, and the afternoon temperature reached sixty-seven degrees. Another Canadian Pacific liner, the Minnedosa, out west of Ireland, was reporting fog. The next morning a depression lay off Iceland. For the rest of the week the ship steamed west, toward the Strait of Belle Isle and the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

He had a watch with him, the family says, and it stayed with him for the rest of his life. Inside the case, where a jeweler had marked it, was a single word: Edinburgh.

On Friday, September 13, 1929, the Duchess came up the river. It was a cold, wet day. At Quebec the high was sixty-one degrees, and nearly half an inch of rain fell in the course of the day; at Montreal the day's rain came to almost two-thirds of an inch. The manifest gives Montreal as the place of arrival. His border card gives Quebec.

From there it was the train. On Sunday, September 15, 1929, he crossed from Windsor into the United States at Detroit, Michigan. At the weather station in Wayne County the overnight low was thirty-four degrees and the afternoon high seventy-two, and the day was dry.

The inspector filled out a card for him, number 21 in the Canadian Pacific series. It records him as Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, single, grocer, Scottish, born in Edinburgh, last residence Dunfermline, bound for Chicago. He had paid his own passage. He had fifty dollars. He had never been in the United States before.

The card also describes him. He was about six feet tall. His hair was fair. His complexion was fair. His eyes were blue.

It is the earliest description of him known to survive. Two more would follow, from the inspector at Blaine, Washington, when he came back across the Canadian border in 1941, and from the clerk who took down his petition for citizenship in 1943.

Six feet. Fair hair. Blue eyes. Fifty dollars. Twenty-two years old, his sister beside him.

Six weeks later Wall Street crashed.

chapters.label: Chapter 22
chapters.title: The Lodger on Kostner Avenue
chapters.html:
He went to his sister's flat on South Kostner Avenue.

Chicago in 1930 was the second-largest city in America, three and a third million people, the hog butcher and railroad hub of the nation. The elevated trains thundered over the streets on iron trestles. The stockyards on the South Side gave off a smell the whole city knew when the wind blew from the southwest. The Loop was a canyon of skyscrapers, the new Merchandise Mart was going up on the river, and on Michigan Avenue the Wrigley Building and the Tribune Tower stood floodlit at night.

The West Side where the Crombies lived was a city of its own. North Lawndale had filled up in the twenty years before with Jewish families who had climbed out of the old Maxwell Street ghetto, and on Roosevelt Road there were kosher butchers, delicatessens, bakeries, Yiddish theaters, and synagogues with tall columns along Douglas Boulevard. The district's great park was Douglas Park, named for Stephen A. Douglas, the senator who had debated Lincoln. A mile or so east, on Homan Avenue, stood the headquarters of Sears, Roebuck and Company, a city of brick buildings and a tall tower where thousands of clerks filled the catalog orders of rural America. The Douglas Park branch of the "L" ran through the south of the district, a few blocks below Kostner's 1500 block, and carried people downtown.

On Kostner Avenue the houses were frame two-flats and cottages with wooden porches and small yards. In summer people sat out on the front steps late into the night because the flats were too hot to sleep in. The iceman came with his wagon and his tongs, and the ragman called from his cart.

Within weeks of his arrival the stock market had broken. In the year after the crash factories laid off men by the thousand, banks began to fail, and breadlines appeared on the streets of Chicago. Al Capone opened a soup kitchen on South State Street.

He kept working. On the 1930 census, taken that April, the Crombie household on South Kostner Avenue, Ward 23, runs across two pages. The enumerator spelled the family name "Crumbie" and wrote Janet as "Jennette". Thomas Crombie was the head of the house and sold furniture. The rent was thirty-two dollars a month. On the second page, at the top, is the lodger: Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, single, a salesman in a grocery, born in Scotland, arrived in 1929, able to read and write English.

The census taker gave the house number as 1532. Every immigration paper that gives the address, written by different hands in 1929 and 1930, has 1534. This book uses 1534.

He was still Lawrence Brown on paper. That would change that autumn. In September 1930 a young woman from Ayr, crossing the border at Port Huron, gave Janet Crombie's address on South Kostner Avenue as her destination.

chapters.label: Chapter 23
chapters.title: The Soldier's Daughter from India
chapters.html:
Helen Ena Harrison was a soldier's child, and she had been born a long way from Scotland.

Bareilly, where she was born, was a cantonment town on the plains of the United Provinces, about a hundred and forty miles east of Delhi: a city of bazaars and mosques and temples, with a British garrison laid out beside it in straight lines of whitewashed barracks, a parade ground, a church, and a cemetery for the soldiers' wives and children who died of fever and cholera. In June, when Helen was born, the heat on the plains could pass a hundred and ten degrees in the shade. A colour sergeant was one of the senior non-commissioned officers of his company, responsible for its stores, its accounts and its colors.

Her father, Richard Harrison, was born in Birmingham, England, about 1872, and went into the army. Her mother, Ada Elizabeth Townsend, was the daughter of Andrew Isaac Townsend, an engine fitter at the Chatham naval dockyard, and grew up in Gillingham, Kent; in 1881, aged three, she was living with her parents at 9 Canterbury Street, New Brompton. Richard and Ada married in the Medway district in the spring of 1899. On the census night of 1901 Ada was back in her parents' house on Rock Avenue, Gillingham. Her husband was away with his regiment.

The regiment was the 1st Battalion, Royal Scots Fusiliers. Their first child, Claud Richard, was born about 1904 at Aldershot. Then the battalion went to India. Helen was born at Bareilly, in the United Provinces, on June 26, 1907, twelve days after Laurence was born in Edinburgh, and baptized there on July 7. Her brother Frank Andrew followed at Bareilly on October 9, 1908. By the spring of 1911 the battalion had moved again, to South Africa. On census night, April 2, 1911, the family was enumerated at Roberts Heights, outside Pretoria: Richard, thirty-nine, colour sergeant; Ada, thirty-three; Claud, seven; Helen Ena, three; Frank, two; and a baby, Alexander Edward, three months, born in the Transvaal.

When war came, the battalion went to France with the British Expeditionary Force. In October 1914 Regimental Quartermaster-Sergeant R. Harrison, number 2933, 1st Royal Scots Fusiliers, was mentioned in despatches for the fighting at Mons, the Marne and the Aisne. By the spring of 1915 an R. Harrison of the Royal Scots Fusiliers, almost certainly her father, held a commission. The London Gazette tracks him upward: temporary lieutenant in March 1915, lieutenant that September, assistant instructor at a school of musketry in 1916, acting captain, and in November 1919 substantive captain with seniority from New Year's Day 1918. He had come up from the ranks to captain. Helen was seven when he went to France, and eleven when the war ended.

After the war the Harrisons settled in Ayr, the regiment's home town on the Firth of Clyde: a seaside town at the mouth of the river Ayr, with long sands, a promenade, a racecourse, and the cottage at Alloway, two miles south, where Robert Burns was born. In 1930 the family lived at 5 Inverkar Road. Later they moved along the road to number 1.

At twenty-three she was five feet six inches tall, with a fair complexion, brown eyes and dark brown hair. She gave her work as housekeeper. How she came to know Janet Crombie, who had left Dunfermline for Chicago in 1926, no record says. But by the summer of 1930 she had decided to go to America, and Janet was the person she was going to.

chapters.label: Chapter 24
chapters.title: Friend: Mrs. Janet Crombie
chapters.html:
Two documents, seven days apart, are almost all that survives of how Helen Harrison and Laurence Douglas came to be married.

On Friday, September 5, 1930, Helen Harrison sailed from Glasgow on the Anchor-Donaldson liner Athenia. At Renfrew, outside Glasgow, the day was breezy and squally, with a little early rain and then sunshine, and the southwest wind blowing at about fifteen miles an hour.

America in September 1930 was sliding into the Depression. Unemployment had more than doubled in a year. In Chicago, men who had worked all their lives stood in line for soup, and Herbert Hoover told the country that the worst was over. A woman arriving from Scotland with no job waiting was taking a chance, and the inspector would note that she had paid her own passage.

She landed at Quebec on Saturday, September 13. It was a raw day there; the thermometer never got above fifty-two degrees.

From Quebec the train ran west through Ontario to Sarnia, at the foot of Lake Huron, where the St. Clair River divides Canada from Michigan. There was no road bridge yet; the Blue Water Bridge would not open for eight more years. Trains crossed under the river through the Grand Trunk Railway's St. Clair Tunnel, an iron tube more than a mile long, opened in 1891.

On Monday, September 15, 1930, a year to the day after Laurence crossed at Detroit, she was inspected at Port Huron, Michigan. The inspector filled out card number 161. Helen Ena Harrison, twenty-two, single. By her date of birth she was twenty-three; the card says twenty-two. He wrote her occupation as housekeeper, then crossed it out and wrote domestic. Able to read and write. Complexion fair. Eyes brown. Hair dark brown. Height five feet six inches. Passage paid by herself. Intending to stay. Her father: Richard Harrison, 5 Inverkar Road, Ayr. Someone had first written her birthplace as Lucknow and crossed it out for Bareilly.

In the space for the person she was joining in the United States, she gave a name and an address: "Friend: Mrs. Janet Crombie, 1534 South Kostner Avenue, Chicago."

That April the census had recorded Laurence as the lodger in Janet's household.

Seven days after the inspection at Port Huron, the Cook County marriage index records the marriage of Lawrence B. Douglas and Helen E. Harrison, on Monday, September 22, 1930, under license number 1291873. At the University of Chicago weather station it was a warm, dry day, seventy-five degrees, with thunder in the afternoon but no measurable rain. He was twenty-three. So was she.

He had entered America as Lawrence Brown. He married as Lawrence B. Douglas. It is the earliest American record I have found to give him the name he had used at school in Dunfermline.

How long he and Helen had known each other, whether they had met in Scotland, and who stood up with them that Monday are not recorded. The seven days measure the time between her inspection at the border and the wedding, not the length of their acquaintance. What the records do show is that Janet links them: Helen named her as the friend she was joining, and Laurence had been living in Janet's household that spring.

chapters.label: Chapter 25
chapters.title: The Depression Years
chapters.html:
They married at the start of the hardest years America has ever known.

Those years left their mark on everyone who lived through them. By the winter of 1932–33 more than a third of Chicago's workforce had no job, and for months the city paid its schoolteachers in scrip or not at all.

The Crombies' stretch of Kostner Avenue was in North Lawndale, a district that had been Bohemian and by 1930 was the largest Jewish neighborhood in Chicago, a hundred and twelve thousand people in greystones, two-flats and frame cottages. Kostner Avenue had been called Forty-fourth Avenue until 1913. The house at 1534 where Janet had lived in 1930 was a frame house built in 1888. The house at 1518, a few doors north, was a two-story, two-apartment frame building of 1898, with a full basement and an attic under the roof.

Laurence kept working, though the records do not say where, and by 1934 he and Helen had a home of their own at 1518 South Kostner Avenue.

On May 18, 1934, Helen left the United States for Scotland. No death, illness or wedding in her family has been found to explain the trip. She stayed six months. On Friday, November 16, 1934, she sailed back from Glasgow on the Letitia, and landed at Quebec on November 25. The manifest records her as Helen Ena Douglas, twenty-seven, married, housewife. She carried a hundred dollars and had paid her own fare. She named her father as Captain Richard Harrison, 1 Inverkar Road, Ayr. She named her husband as Laurence Douglas, 1518 South Kostner Avenue, Chicago.

Apart from the census of 1911, taken when he was three, it is one of the first records to spell his first name the way he would spell it for the rest of his life.

In the family it was remembered that he was lonely while Helen was away.

On October 3, 1936, Janet gave birth to twin daughters, Elizabeth and Jessie. Elizabeth was called Betty. Laurence was an uncle at twenty-nine.

Sometime between the spring of 1935 and the end of 1936, Laurence left Chicago for Providence, Rhode Island. By 1937 he would have a new trade there, as a display man, dressing the windows of a store on Weybosset Street. It would be his work for the rest of his life.

In January 1937 Helen sailed for Scotland again. When she came back, in May 1938, the husband she named on the manifest was living in Providence.

chapters.label: Chapter 26
chapters.title: The Display Man of Weybosset Street
chapters.html:
By 1937 Laurence was in Providence, Rhode Island, and he was a display manager.

The Providence city directory for 1937 lists a Lawrence Douglas, display manager, very probably Laurence, working at 165 Weybosset Street, in the heart of the downtown shopping district, and rooming at 35 Elmwood Avenue. The directory for 1938 lists him again, at the same job and the same address on Weybosset, now rooming at 458 Pine Street.

Number 165 was the John Mason Building, six stories of brick over a steel frame, designed by the Providence firm of Stone, Carpenter and Willson and built in 1903. Across the street stood the Outlet Company, the city's great department store, which by then filled most of a block and broadcast its own radio station, WJAR, from inside the store.

Providence was a city of about two hundred and fifty thousand people, the capital of the smallest state and the center of one of the most industrial corners of the country. Rhode Island made textiles in mills along all its rivers, machine tools at Brown and Sharpe, files at Nicholson and silverware at Gorham, and in the brick factories of the Jewelry District south of downtown thousands of women soldered and polished the rings, pins and compacts that let Providence call itself the jewelry capital of the world.

Its people came downtown to shop. Westminster and Weybosset Streets, running side by side a block apart, were lined with department stores, specialty shops, banks, theaters and lunch counters. On Westminster stood the Shepard Company, the biggest store in the city, whose clock over the corner was where Rhode Islanders arranged to meet; Gladding's, which called itself the oldest dry-goods store in America; Cherry and Webb; and the jewelers Tilden-Thurber, at the corner of Mathewson Street. Between the two streets ran the Arcade of 1828, a granite Greek temple with three floors of small shops under a glass roof. At the east end, where the two streets met, the sixteen-story Turk's Head Building rose over the traffic like the prow of a ship, and behind it stood the Industrial Trust building, twenty-six stories of limestone finished in 1928, the tallest building in New England.

And everywhere there were windows. In the 1930s the store window was the most important advertising a merchant had. A man walking down Weybosset Street could look into fifty of them in ten minutes: mannequins in fall suits against painted autumn woods, a pyramid of new radios, a bride and her attendants, Christmas windows with moving figures that drew crowds three deep. The men who made them were called display men or window trimmers, and the best of them were paid as artists.

The clothes on their mannequins were the clothes of the late thirties. For men: broad-shouldered double-breasted suits in chalk stripe and glen check, high-waisted trousers with deep pleats and cuffs, wide silk ties, two-tone wingtips and snap-brim fedoras. For women: bias-cut dresses that clung and flowed, shoulders padded wider every season, hats tilted over one eye, fox furs, gloves to the wrist and seamed silk stockings.

In the family, the thing everyone remembered about Laurence was how he looked. He was never less than impeccably dressed: a good suit, carefully pressed; a white shirt; the tie knotted just so; polished shoes; his hair combed perfectly into place. It was the look of the man and the look of his trade. A display man was in the business of making things look right.

At five o'clock on a weekday the heart of downtown was Exchange Place, the open square in front of City Hall that a later generation would rename Kennedy Plaza. Every streetcar line in the city met there. The cars of the United Electric Railways came in from Olneyville and Elmwood and Smith Hill, from Pawtucket and Cranston and East Providence, and pulled up in lines at the loading islands; the newer trackless trolleys glided in beside them on rubber tires, and the cars for the East Side ducked into the tunnel under College Hill. Clerks and stenographers in hats and gloves, jewelry workers with lunch pails, salesgirls from the Outlet and Shepard's and newsboys shouting the evening Bulletin crowded onto the cars. At the head of the square stood Union Station, where the New Haven Railroad's trains left for Boston and New York.

Laurence was alone in those years. Helen's own papers say that from 1930 to 1937 she lived in the United States, and that her last home there was Rhode Island. On December 19, 1936, she was issued a re-entry permit, number 1123011, in Washington. On about January 10, 1937, she sailed for Scotland again.

Three weeks later, on January 31, 1937, her grandfather Andrew Isaac Townsend, a retired dockyard engine fitter, died. The probate calendar gives his address as her parents' house, 1 Inverkar Road, Ayr. Helen stayed in Scotland for fifteen months.

The Providence directories of both years list Laurence by himself. A directory of the period normally printed a married man's wife's name in parentheses after his own; there is no name after Laurence's. In both years the letter beside his home address is "r", for one who roomed or boarded, not "h", for a householder: a rented room on Elmwood Avenue in 1937, another on Pine Street in 1938. The family remembered that he was lonely while Helen was away. He was a heavy smoker, like most men of his day, and he loved to read; the Providence Public Library, in its marble building at Empire and Washington Streets, was a short walk from Weybosset Street.

Elmwood, where he took his first room, was a neighborhood of big Queen Anne and Shingle Style houses built in the 1880s and 1890s by mill owners, jewelry manufacturers and merchants when the streetcar first came out that way, with turrets, wraparound porches and stained glass on the stair landings. At the far end of Elmwood Avenue lay Roger Williams Park, more than four hundred acres of lakes, lawns and woods. On summer Sundays families came out on the streetcars with picnic baskets, rented rowboats on the lakes and sat on the grass for the band concerts at the Temple to Music, a white marble temple on the shore.

Helen came back in the spring of 1938. On Saturday, April 23, she sailed from Glasgow on the Anchor liner Cameronia, and she reached New York on Monday, May 2, 1938. The manifest lists her as Helen Ena Douglas, thirty, married, housewife, born at Bareilly, India, carrying fifty dollars, last permanent residence Providence. She named her father as Captain Richard Harrison, 1 Inverkar Road, Ayr. She named her husband as Lawrence Brown Douglas, 351 Friendship Street, Providence.

It is the last known record in which Helen named Laurence as her husband. The next record of hers to name him, twelve years later and an ocean away, would say that she had divorced him. The address she gave was not the one in his directory listing that year. In 1940 the house at 351 Friendship Street was the home of Edmund Lucas, a lieutenant in the Providence Fire Department, and no Douglas lived there.

Westminster Street ran parallel to Weybosset, one block north. In the same two years a young hairdresser worked there: at number 280 in 1937, and at number 300, room 402, in 1938. Her workplace and Laurence's were a few minutes' walk apart. Her name was Constance Eugenie Darcy.

chapters.label: Chapter 27
chapters.title: The Printer's Daughter
chapters.html:
While Laurence was still a small boy in Scotland, the woman he would spend the rest of his life with was born on the other side of the ocean, in Providence, into a family of printers.

Her father, Albert Blake Darcy, was born on November 20, 1888, in East Providence, in the village of Rumford, the first child of John F. and Maggie Darcy. His father's family had come from Ireland. Rumford was a village built around the Rumford Chemical Works, whose baking powder was sold in grocery stores all over America. In 1900 the family lived on Orchard Street, East Providence. By 1910, at twenty-one, Albert was an apprentice on a Monotype machine, learning to set type.

His was a new trade. The Linotype, first used at a New York newspaper in 1886, and the Monotype that followed it set type from a keyboard and cast it in hot lead, and they had turned the printing business upside down. A good operator was a skilled and well-paid man, and on a morning paper he worked nights in the clatter and heat of the composing room so that the paper could be on the doorsteps at dawn.

On January 16, 1912, in Providence, Albert Blake Darcy, twenty-three, printer, married Eugenie Emma Delaire, seventeen, the daughter of Timothy and Julia Delaire. A Roman Catholic priest, William Pyne, married them. The record gives the bride's birthplace as Sutton, Quebec. She was one of the many thousands of French Canadians whose families had come down from Quebec to the mill towns of New England.

Their first child was born on Saturday, October 12, 1912, at 410 Smith Street, Providence, on the street that runs up past the white marble State House. They named her Constance Eugenie. Eugenie's mother, Julia Delaire, a widow, was boarding in the same house the next year.

Albert moved where the work was. In 1914 the Providence directory noted that he had "removed to Boston". By December 1915 the family was in Taunton, Massachusetts, where a son, Albert Norman, was born on the seventh. By June 1917 they were back in Providence, at 8 Esten Street, and Albert was a linotype operator for the Pawtucket Times. When he registered for the draft that June he was described as tall and of medium build, with light blue eyes and dark brown hair, and he listed a wife, two children and his mother-in-law as dependents. In 1920 the family rented at 19 Alma Street, Providence; in 1925, at 29 Pawtucket Avenue, East Providence.

The marriage did not last. In April 1930 Eugenie was the head of her own household at 111 Pratt Street, Providence, divorced, working as an interior decorator at a rug works and paying twenty-eight dollars a month in rent, with a radio in the flat. Constance, seventeen, was in school. Her father remarried; his second wife was Theresa B. Sullivan, and they settled at Shawomet, in Warwick. By the late 1930s he was a compositor for the Providence Journal.

Constance grew up between those households. In 1934 she was a student, living at 7 Beacon Avenue. Then she trained as a hairdresser. A Rhode Island state census card made about January 1936 records her at 75 Abbott Street, Providence: born October 12, 1912, single, hairdresser, at work. Her mother, Mrs. Eugenie E. Darcy, kept house at the same address. By 1937 Constance was rooming at 11 Grand View and working at 280 Westminster Street. By 1938 she and her mother lived at 56 Dartmouth Avenue, and she worked at 300 Westminster Street, room 402.

She had come of age with the beauty parlor. In the 1920s women all over America had cut their hair short, and the new bobs needed cutting every few weeks; then came the finger wave, the marcel and the permanent wave, set with hot irons and with electric machines that hung over the client's head and clamped a curler to every lock. A girl who trained as a hairdresser in the 1930s learned all of it, and she worked all day in a shop full of women talking, with the driers humming and the radio on. The film stars set the styles: Jean Harlow's platinum waves, Claudette Colbert's bangs, Myrna Loy's soft curls.

In the family, Constance is remembered for her nature. She was pleasant and congenial, easy to be with, the kind of woman who put the people around her at ease. Those were gifts for a beauty parlor, and they served her just as well later, when she became a nurse. Like Laurence, she was a heavy smoker. Her grandchildren, of whom I am one, called her Nan.

When she and Laurence met, and how, no one wrote down. Their first daughter was born on February 10, 1939. By about May 1938, the month Helen landed in New York and named Laurence as her husband, Constance and Laurence were already together.

chapters.label: Chapter 28
chapters.title: The Hurricane of 1938
chapters.html:
Wednesday, September 21, 1938, began in Providence like an ordinary working day.

It had rained for four days. The ground was soaked and the rivers were high. The morning came up sunny, and by ten o'clock clouds were rolling in from the south. People came downtown on the streetcars as they did every day, to work and to look in the windows of stores where, nine years into the Depression, many of them could not afford to buy.

That year's directory placed Laurence, display manager, at 165 Weybosset Street, in the Mason Building across from the Outlet Company, and Constance Darcy, hairdresser, a block north at 300 Westminster Street, room 402. Both streets ran east, downhill, to the Turk's Head Building at the point where they met, and beyond it to Exchange Place, the Biltmore Hotel, City Hall, Market Square and the river. Downtown Providence stood at the head of Narragansett Bay, at the narrow end of a funnel nearly thirty miles long.

No one in the city had been told that a hurricane was coming. The storm had been tracked up the Atlantic coast for days, but the forecasters in Washington expected it to curve harmlessly out to sea. Instead it ran north at about fifty miles an hour, crossed Long Island in the afternoon and came ashore again on the Connecticut coast near Milford, at the time of the equinox and close to the hour of astronomical high tide.

By about two o'clock the wind in Providence was blowing hard, and the city went on with its plans. At the Narragansett Hotel on Dorrance Street a wedding was set for that evening; when the Providence Journal's society editor telephoned to ask whether it would go ahead, the bride, Loraine Fogel, said it would.

Around three o'clock the real wind arrived. People who heard it said it sounded like a train. Plate glass began to go. On one downtown street the whole front window of a furniture store came out in a single sheet and was carried up the street, shattering as it went. All over the business district there was a steady popping, the sound of windows bursting from their frames.

Late in the afternoon the sea broke over the Rhode Island shore. At Westerly and Watch Hill, at Misquamicut, Charlestown and Narragansett, the surge swept whole rows of summer cottages into the ocean with people still inside them. Then the water came up the bay. The southerly gale held the high tide in and kept driving more water north, past Newport, past Prudence Island, where the lighthouse keeper's wife and son and neighbors who had sheltered with them were drowned, past Warwick and Edgewood, into the throat of the Providence River.

Just as the offices and stores of downtown let out, at about five o'clock, the surge reached the city. It came first up through the sewers; then the river came over its banks and poured west into the business district. In Exchange Place, in front of City Hall, water that had been a few inches deep was waist deep within minutes. At about five o'clock the anemometer at the Providence Weather Bureau office was blown away after recording winds of eighty-seven miles an hour. The National Weather Service now credits Providence with sustained winds of a hundred miles an hour and a gust of a hundred and twenty-five.

The flood ran up Weybosset Street and through the doors of its shops. Parked cars were lifted and carried toward the river. Streetcars stood abandoned in water up to their windows. As the water reached the wiring of the parked cars, their horns began to sound and kept sounding, and people who heard it remembered it as the strangest sound of the day. Into the streets came the wreckage of the upper bay: boats torn from their moorings, oil barrels, timbers and the stock of the downtown stores.

People caught outdoors climbed anything that stood above the water. They crowded the steps of City Hall. At the Biltmore Hotel, bedsheets were thrown down from the second floor to people in the water. The Hope Club, which did not admit women, took women in. In the office buildings and stores, those who had not yet left went up to the higher floors and watched the water fill the floors below. Some who stayed in their cars drowned in them; others were knocked down by the current near City Hall.

The water crested at thirteen feet eight and a half inches above mean high water, as marked on the Market House at Market Square, one foot eleven and a quarter inches above the mark of the Great Gale of September 23, 1815, the city's worst flood until that night.

Where Laurence and Constance were that afternoon, no record says. The directories place their workplaces a block apart on the two streets the water reached. They do not say whether either was at work that Wednesday, where either sheltered, or how either got home.

By about half past five the wind had dropped. The storm, still racing north, was already over Massachusetts on its way to Vermont. In the dark the water began to drain back toward the bay almost as fast as it had come.

That night downtown was dark. The wedding at the Narragansett Hotel went ahead late in the evening by candlelight; the groom had been stranded for hours at Union Station, and strangers caught by the storm had eaten the wedding supper. Looting had begun while the water was still high, and National Guard troops were sent to patrol the city.

At daylight on Thursday the city came back to see what was left. The streets of downtown were full of drowned automobiles, boats, broken glass and ruined merchandise. The steamer Monhegan lay sunk at Fox Point, at the head of the harbor. The stores and offices of Westminster and Weybosset Streets would be digging out for two weeks.

The day after the storm the Providence Journal counted ninety dead in Rhode Island. The full count, which took many days, was close to four hundred, most of them along the shore. For southern New England as a whole, the National Weather Service gives 564 deaths, at least 1,700 injuries and 8,900 homes, cottages and buildings destroyed; other tallies run higher. Property damage across New England was estimated at roughly three hundred million dollars at 1938 prices.

A hurricane barrier across the Providence River at Fox Point, built to keep the sea out of downtown, was not finished until 1966, five years after Laurence's death.

The water went down. The city counted its dead, swept out its stores and put its windows back in.

chapters.label: Chapter 29
chapters.title: A Wedding in Alabama
chapters.html:
On Friday, February 10, 1939, Constance gave birth to a daughter at Attleboro, in Bristol County, Massachusetts, a jewelry-making town just across the state line from Pawtucket. The child was named Eugenie Elizabeth. Eugenie was the name of Constance's mother; Elizabeth was the name of the woman who had raised Laurence.

Eight months later, on Monday, October 9, 1939, Laurence and Constance were married in Birmingham, Alabama, about a thousand miles from Providence.

The world went to war in between. On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. On Sunday, September 3, Britain and France declared war. That evening, northwest of Ireland, a German submarine torpedoed the liner Athenia, outward bound from Glasgow for Montreal with more than eleven hundred passengers, many of them Americans and Canadians leaving Europe. More than a hundred people died. The Athenia was the first British ship sunk in the Second World War. It was also the ship on which Helen had sailed for America nine years before.

Laurence was still a British subject. Five weeks later he was married in a country at peace. Birmingham was the steel city of the South, called the Magic City for how fast it had grown, with the blast furnaces of Sloss glowing along the valley at night and the iron statue of Vulcan on Red Mountain above the city. It was also a city where the law kept Black and white citizens apart on the streetcars, at the lunch counters and in the waiting rooms.

The Weather Bureau station at the Birmingham airport recorded a high of eighty-eight degrees that day, in the middle of a dry spell. The Jefferson County Courthouse was new, finished in 1932: a tall Art Deco building of granite and limestone by the Chicago architects Holabird and Root, facing Woodrow Wilson Park (today's Linn Park), its walls carved with panels of the county's history and its lobby painted with murals of the Old South and the New. In the office of the probate judge a clerk filled in the right-hand entry on page 409 of the marriage license ledger: the application, a physician's certificate, a bond, the license and the return, all dated the same day.

The groom gave his name as Lawrence Douglas, thirty-two, born in Edinburgh, a salesman. For his home he did not give Providence. He gave 1860 South Hamlin Avenue, Chicago: his sister Janet's address. For his parents he wrote Robert Douglas and Elizabeth McDonald. The bride gave her name as Constance Eugenie Darcy, twenty-six, three days short of her twenty-seventh birthday, born in Providence, of 454 Broadway, Providence. For her parents she wrote Albert B. Darcy and Eugenie Delaire. The bond was co-signed by a man whose name reads T. B. Pickens. They were married by Thos. R. Lea, judge of the Municipal Court.

The next day their names appeared in two Birmingham papers, the Birmingham Post and the Age-Herald.

Laurence had married Helen in Chicago nine years earlier, and seventeen months before the Birmingham wedding Helen had named him as her husband when she landed in New York. For a long time I could find no divorce. Then, in the marriage register of Ayr for 1950, I found Helen's own account. When she married again that August, she described herself as formerly married to Laurence Brown Douglas, "against whom she obtained Decree of Divorce." So there was a divorce, and it was Helen who sought it.

The register does not say when the decree was granted, or in what court. Whether it came before this wedding in Birmingham or after it, I do not yet know. Nor does any record say why the marriage ended, and I will not guess.

The address Constance gave, 454 Broadway, was on one of the handsome old streets of Providence. Broadway ran west from downtown above Federal Hill, a wide avenue with a streetcar line, lined in the decades after the Civil War with the Italianate, Second Empire and Queen Anne houses of the city's newly rich. By the 1930s many of them had been divided into flats and rooms.

Less than four years later, in the naturalization petition he signed in federal court at Pittsburgh, Laurence described Constance as his second wife. He did not hide that there had been a first.

Laurence was thirty-two and Constance was twenty-six. They were married for twenty-one years, until his death in March 1961.

chapters.label: Chapter 30
chapters.title: California
chapters.html:
They were young, and they went west.

When Laurence and Constance married in Birmingham, Alabama, on October 9, 1939, he gave an address in Chicago and she gave one in Providence. Six months later they were living in San Francisco with their daughter Eugenie, at the far edge of the continent. The records do not say when they went or how they traveled.

San Francisco in 1940 was the most beautiful city in America, and it knew it. The Golden Gate Bridge had opened in 1937 and the Bay Bridge the year before, and out on Treasure Island the Golden Gate International Exposition was running its second season, with its Tower of the Sun and its Pageant of the Pacific. Cable cars clanged up Powell Street past Union Square and the Dewey Monument, and around the square and the blocks beside it stood the great stores: the City of Paris, the White House, Gump's. On Market Street four lines of streetcar track ran side by side. In summer the fog came in through the Golden Gate in the afternoons and lay over the city like wool, and the foghorns sounded from the bay all night.

The Mission District, where they lived, was the warm, sunny side of the city, out of the worst of the fog. It was a working neighborhood of Irish, German and Italian families, of wooden flats with bay windows built after the earthquake and fire of 1906, of corner bars and bakeries and big parish churches. Mission Street was its main street, lined with movie theaters and furniture stores; at Sixteenth and Dolores stood Mission Dolores, completed by the Spanish in 1791, the oldest building in the city. Not far off, the Seals played baseball at Seals Stadium.

On Thursday, April 11, 1940, a census taker came to their flat on Valencia Street and wrote down three people: Laurence Douglas, thirty-two, born in Scotland; Constance, twenty-seven, born in Rhode Island; and a daughter, one year old, born in Massachusetts. Laurence was a window trimmer in retail clothing. He had worked forty-eight hours the week before and fifty-two weeks of 1939, and had earned two thousand two hundred and forty dollars, about forty-three dollars a week. The rent was thirty-three dollars a month. For 1935 the census recorded Chicago for him and Providence for her.

The employer was Bond Stores, the men's clothing chain. Founded in Cleveland in 1914, Bond had grown by 1940 into one of the largest men's clothiers in the country, known for its two-trouser suits and its windows; that year it opened a store on Times Square. Its San Francisco store stood at Post and Kearny Streets, in the downtown shopping district two blocks east of Union Square. Its windows were Laurence's.

On Wednesday, October 16, 1940, the first national registration day, more than sixteen million American men between twenty-one and thirty-five signed up at schools, firehouses and draft board offices across the country. Laurence signed card serial number 3426 at Local Board 94, 513 Valencia Street. He gave his home as 129 Julian Avenue, a four-story building of seven flats put up in 1916 on a short street a block off Valencia; his employer as Bond Stores, Inc., Post and Kearny; and the person who would always know his address as his wife, Constance. The same day, on the other side of the country in Warwick, Rhode Island, Constance's younger brother, Albert Norman Darcy, twenty-four, signed his own card and named his wife, Claire.

The 1941 San Francisco directory carries him at the same address: Lawrence L. Douglas, displayman, Bond Clothes, wife Constance E., 129 Julian. The store's own listing names its manager, Carl Allison, and its telephone, YUkon 0585.

In early June 1941 Laurence obtained a re-entry permit, issued in Washington on June 2. On June 20 he left the country, and the next day, Saturday, June 21, 1941, he came back across the Canadian border at Blaine, Washington, by motor stage, with Constance. He had turned thirty-four a week earlier, though the inspector put him down as thirty-three. The inspector recorded him as Lawrence Brown Douglas, displayman, about six feet tall, brown hair, blue eyes, returning to resume residence with his wife, Constance, a United States citizen. Their destination was 17-B Mirabel Avenue, San Francisco, one of two flats in a two-story house of 1905 near the foot of Bernal Heights. He had been in the United States for nearly twelve years. The next day, June 22, Germany invaded the Soviet Union.

Their second daughter, Constance Anderson Douglas, was born in San Francisco on February 2. The state's birth index gives the year as 1941; her father's citizenship petition gives 1942. She carried her mother's first name. Her middle name, Anderson, was the surname then used by Elizabeth, the woman who had raised Laurence in Scotland. Both records agree on the city and the day.

chapters.label: Chapter 31
chapters.title: Pearl Harbor: The Sirens of San Francisco
chapters.html:
San Francisco Chronicle
Japan Planes Near S.F. — 4 Raid Alarms
Tuesday, December 9, 1941

In December 1941, San Francisco spent its nights in the dark, waiting to be bombed.

That autumn the Douglas family was divided. In the family it was remembered that from about September 1941 Laurence was working in the Pittsburgh district while his wife, Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas, remained in San Francisco, and two Pittsburgh men later swore that they had known him since that September. No record says where each of them was on December 7, or why they were living apart.

Sunday, December 7, began like any Sunday in San Francisco. The churches of the Mission were full for the late Masses, and families walked in Golden Gate Park. At 7:48 that morning, Hawaii time, the first wave of Japanese carrier planes came in over Oahu and fell on the Pacific Fleet at anchor in Pearl Harbor. The first reports reached San Francisco a little before half past eleven. The radio broke into its programs, and people came out of their houses and stood in the street asking each other whether it was true. Through the afternoon the bulletins were fragmentary and often contradictory. Listeners learned that Pearl Harbor and the airfields of Oahu had been bombed and that there had been heavy damage and loss of life. They could not learn its extent.

At about a quarter past six that evening the city had its first air-raid alarm and its first blackout. The Army's Fourth Interceptor Command reported thirty-odd enemy planes ranging over the bay from San Jose to the Mare Island navy yard, and the region went dark for hours. Radio stations were ordered off the air during the alerts, so that enemy pilots could not use their signals to find the city. The city was not ready. It had almost no air-raid sirens; the Ferry Building had one, and police cars and fire engines raced through the streets with their own sirens to spread the alarm, while volunteer wardens went door to door shouting at people to turn out their lights. The great neon signs on Market Street were on time switches, and no one could turn them off. People in the streets said they heard the drone of motors overhead, and dogfights out over the ocean. The sirens sounded four times that night. No bombs fell. The planes, if there were planes, were never found. On Tuesday morning the Chronicle's headline read: Japan Planes Near S.F. — 4 Raid Alarms.

No bomb ever fell on San Francisco.

In 1943 Laurence's citizenship papers place both daughters with him in Avalon, Pennsylvania. Between the sirens on the Pacific coast and that address above the Ohio River, the family left no account of the journey east.

chapters.label: Chapter 32
chapters.title: Citizen Douglas
chapters.html:
In the middle of a world war, a man whose Edinburgh birth entry had no father's name in it became, in a federal court in Pittsburgh, a citizen of the United States.

Pittsburgh at war was the arsenal of democracy, and it looked it. Along the Monongahela and the Ohio the steel mills of Jones and Laughlin, Carnegie-Illinois and a dozen others ran day and night, the mill whistles marking every change of shift, and the smoke was so thick that on winter days the streetlights sometimes burned at noon. The mills poured out armor plate, shells, landing craft and the steel for ships and tanks.

Avalon lay a few miles down the Ohio from the city, on the hillside above the river, a quiet borough of brick and frame houses, churches and corner stores, with the Pennsylvania Railroad running along the riverbank below. Families planted victory gardens, saved tin cans and fat for the war effort, and hung service flags in their windows. From May 1942 sugar was rationed, and gasoline; that November, coffee. Every family had its ration books.

By February 1943 Laurence was display manager for Bond Stores in Pittsburgh and was living at 612 California Avenue, Avalon, a two-story brick building of about 1900 with a storefront or office at street level and rooms above. His two daughters were living there with him.

On February 11, 1943, nine days after the last German forces at Stalingrad surrendered, Laurence petitioned for naturalization in the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania. His petition, number 139903, sets out his particulars. Laurence Brown Douglas. Display manager, Bond Stores. Born Edinburgh, June 14, 1907. British nationality. Complexion fair, eyes blue, hair brown. Five feet eleven inches. One hundred and fifty-two pounds. No visible distinctive marks. Arrived at Detroit on September 15, 1929, under the name Lawrence Brown. It gives his last foreign residence as Ayr and his port of emigration as Glasgow, although the records of 1929 give Dunfermline and Greenock.

For his wife he gave Constance Darcy, married at Birmingham, Alabama, on October 9, 1939, born at Providence. Beside her name the form records her as his second wife. For his children he gave two daughters, both living with him at Avalon: Eugenie Elizabeth, born February 10, 1939, at Attleboro, Massachusetts, and Constance Anderson, whose birth he gave as February 2, 1942, at San Francisco.

Two Pittsburgh men, David Hunter, a machinist, and Frank Holliday, a clerk, signed as his witnesses and swore that they had known him since September 1941. His years in California were covered by depositions: on March 3, 1943, in San Francisco, two people who had known him there, William Howard Vahlkamp and Betty Johnstone Sherwood, swore statements for his petition.

On Thursday, May 6, 1943, in the federal court in Pittsburgh, Laurence Brown Douglas took the oath of allegiance and renounced his allegiance to the British Crown. The court granted his petition and admitted him to citizenship. A week later the last Axis forces in North Africa surrendered in Tunisia.

On April 27, 1942, the government registered for the draft every man from forty-five to sixty-four, and Constance's father, Albert Blake Darcy, fifty-three, signed his card in Warwick that day.

The war remade American dress by order. To save cloth, the War Production Board's orders of 1942 banned trouser cuffs for men and ended the two-trouser suit that Bond had built its trade on.

The child registered in Edinburgh in 1907 as Lawrence Brown, son of Agnes, was now, by order of an American court, Laurence Brown Douglas, citizen of the United States.

chapters.label: Chapter 33
chapters.title: Home to Rhode Island
chapters.html:
After the war Laurence brought his family home to Rhode Island, where Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas had grown up and where he had dressed windows on Weybosset Street before the war. He was nearly forty, a citizen, a husband and a father.

Pawtucket was the state's oldest mill city. It was here, at the falls of the Blackstone River, that Samuel Slater had built America's first successful cotton-spinning mill in 1793, and for a century and a half the city had lived by textiles: thread, lace, braid, yarn and cloth made in big brick mills along the river. Its downtown on Main Street was busy with department stores, five-and-tens and movie houses, and on Saturdays the sidewalks were crowded with mill families shopping. On the edge of town McCoy Stadium, opened in 1942, drew crowds for baseball on summer nights.

He went to work for the stores of Pawtucket. In 1947 the Pawtucket directory lists him on page 154: Douglas, Laurence B., wife Constance E., window dresser, home 97 Magill Street. Magill Street, in the Woodlawn section, was a street of wooden two- and three-family houses built between about 1900 and 1920 for mill hands and tradesmen, with porches stacked one above another and clotheslines across the back yards. Woodlawn's families were French Canadian, Irish, Portuguese and Polish, many of them there for two generations. Downtown, along Main Street, were the stores whose windows needed dressing: W. T. Grant, Woolworth's, Kresge's.

By 1950 they had moved into Providence, to 148 General Street, in the North End near the Pawtucket line. The Providence directory for 1950 lists Lawrence B. and Constance at that address. In 1951, 1953 and 1955 the directories list them there again, and give his work in two words: display worker.

There were three daughters now: Eugenie Elizabeth, called Genie; Constance Anderson Douglas; and Norma, the youngest, born after her father's petition of 1943, which names only two. The girls went to Bay View: St. Mary's Academy, Bay View, a Catholic school for girls on the shore of Narragansett Bay in East Providence, run by the Sisters of Mercy, who had founded the academy in 1874. For a Catholic family in Providence it was the school to send a daughter to.

That was the world the Douglas girls grew up in. By the middle of the century Rhode Island had the largest Catholic share of its population of any state, and the Church shaped every part of life from birth to burial: Latin Mass on Sunday, fish on Friday, parochial schools taught by nuns.

On a Saturday, families still dressed up to go into Providence, to the Outlet Company, Shepard's and Gladding's, but every year more of them drove past downtown to the Garden City shopping center in Cranston, opened in 1948. The last streetcar in Providence ran in May 1948; after that it was buses and, more and more, the family car.

On the morning of August 31, 1954, Hurricane Carol came up Narragansett Bay with little warning, and the sea came into downtown Providence again. Water stood feet deep in the downtown streets for the second time in sixteen years; store basements and ground floors were wrecked, and power was out across the state for days. Across New England, by the Weather Bureau's count, Carol destroyed some four thousand homes, three thousand five hundred automobiles and three thousand boats. After Carol the planning began for a hurricane barrier at Fox Point.

Around the family, the older generation was passing. Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas's grandmother, Margaret Jane Darcy, had died at her son Albert's house, 60 Blake Street in Shawomet, on September 10, 1942. Constance's brother, Albert Norman Darcy, died on October 1, 1954, aged thirty-eight, and was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, section 5, lot 84. Her father, Albert Blake Darcy, the linotype man, died on November 4, 1957, sixteen days short of his sixty-ninth birthday, and was buried at Mount Saint Mary Cemetery in Pawtucket.

In Ayr, Helen's mother, Ada Elizabeth Harrison, of 1a Inverkar Road, died on June 10, 1952. In Chicago, Janet and Thomas Crombie had both become American citizens: Thomas on September 9, 1947, Janet on March 16, 1948.

Laurence was in his forties now, with three daughters and a trade.

chapters.label: Chapter 34
chapters.title: The Last House
chapters.html:
By 1956 Laurence and Constance had moved again, a short way across the North End, to 644 River Avenue, Providence. It was the last house he would live in.

River Avenue ran through Elmhurst, a neighborhood of wooden two- and three-family houses with porches stacked one above the other, mostly Irish and Italian, Catholic and working: fathers in the shops, the post office and the fire department, mothers raising big families in six-room flats. Number 644 was one of those houses. The parish was St. Pius V, on Elmhurst Avenue. Farther along, River Avenue ran beside Providence College, which the Dominican friars had founded in 1917, and the friars in their white habits were a familiar sight in the neighborhood. Roger Williams General Hospital, on Chalkstone Avenue, was a short drive away.

The Providence directories of 1956 and 1959 list Laurence B. and Constance E. Douglas at number 644 and give his trade as display. In 1960 the directory is more exact: Douglas, Laurence B. (Constance E.), displayman, Carter's Men Store, Pawtucket, home 644 River Avenue.

It was the same work he had done for a quarter of a century, from Weybosset Street to Post and Kearny to Pittsburgh: the mannequins in suits and topcoats, the hats and ties laid out on risers, the backdrops and price cards, the windows changed for Easter and back-to-school and Christmas. A men's clothing store in a New England mill town in 1960 still sold to people walking past on the sidewalk, and the window was how it spoke to them. The windows of Carter's showed the clothes of a sober, prosperous America: narrow lapels, skinny ties, button-down collars.

In the family he is remembered as impeccably dressed, his suit pressed and his hair perfectly combed, as a man who loved to read, and as a heavy smoker. His wife smoked heavily too. By 1954 the studies linking cigarettes to lung cancer had made the newspapers, and the tobacco companies answered with filter tips and reassuring advertisements. Few people of their generation quit. The Surgeon General's report that told the country plainly what cigarettes did was not published until January 1964, nearly three years after Laurence died.

Their eldest daughter had gone into the Church. Eugenie Elizabeth Douglas entered the Dominican Sisters, whose motherhouse was St. Dominic's Convent at Blauvelt, New York, west of the Hudson. A young woman entering religious life in those years came first as a postulant; after months of prayer and work she was received as a novice, and took the habit of the order and a new name. Genie's was Sister Mary Laurene, a name that echoes her father's.

Constance Eugenie Darcy Douglas had gone to work too. She trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing, and by 1961 she was a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital.

By the time the 1961 directory was compiled, Laurence was working for himself. His listing gives one line: window displays, at 644 River Avenue, home and business at the same address.

The girls were grown. By the beginning of 1961 Constance Anderson Douglas had married and, as Mrs. Constance Garceau, was living in Warwick. Norma was living at home in Providence. Eugenie was Sister Mary Laurene, at St. Dominic's Convent in Blauvelt. In Chicago, Janet's daughter Jessie had married Ronald H. Power in September 1958.

All through Laurence's last years, the industrial Rhode Island that had built Providence was coming apart, as one textile mill after another closed and its owners moved south. For a display man whose living depended on the stores, and for stores whose living depended on mill families with money in their pockets on a Saturday, it meant fewer customers on Main Street in Pawtucket every year, and fewer windows to dress.

Laurence was fifty-three. It was the last house.

chapters.label: Chapter 35
chapters.title: The Ninth of March
chapters.html:
His family understood it to be lung cancer, and it gave them almost no warning. My mother, Constance Anderson Douglas, told me years later that she never knew her father had cancer until he was taken into the hospital. Nobody at home knew. He went in suddenly, and the illness, as his obituary put it, was brief.

He had been a heavy smoker, and so was his wife. In 1961 few cancers of the lung were found early, and there was little a doctor could do for one that was not.

The city where he died was the city he had come to as a young man. Downtown was still busy that winter, though not as busy as it had been. The Outlet and Shepard's still dressed their windows on Weybosset and Westminster Streets. Loew's State Theatre on Weybosset Street still showed the new pictures. The Mason Building, at 165 Weybosset Street, where the directories had placed his work in 1937 and 1938, still stood across from the Outlet. But the streetcars were long gone, replaced by buses, and the new highway was coming through.

On Thursday, March 9, 1961, Laurence Brown Douglas died at St. Joseph's Hospital, the Catholic hospital at 21 Peace Street, at the corner of Broad Street in South Providence. St. Joseph's Hospital had opened in 1892 in the old Harris mansion. By 1961 the mansion stood beside the brick buildings that had grown up around it: a building begun in 1893, a west wing of 1930, an expansion of 1954. The hospital was in the same South Providence neighborhood as Dartmouth Avenue, where Constance Darcy had lived with her mother in 1938. He was fifty-three years, eight months and twenty-three days old.

On Saturday, March 11, the Pawtucket Times printed his obituary on page three. It gave his home as 644 River Avenue. It said he had been born in Edinburgh, Scotland, the son of the late Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. It said he had worked for the Bond Clothing Company, then had his own display business, and that for the past fifteen years he had dressed windows for Pawtucket firms.

It named those who survived him: his wife, Constance E. (Darcy) Douglas; three daughters, Sister Mary Laurene, O.P., of St. Dominic's Convent, Blauvelt, New York, Mrs. Constance Garceau of Warwick, and Miss Norma Douglas of Providence; and a sister, Mrs. Thomas Crombie of Chicago. Sister Mary Laurene was Eugenie Elizabeth Douglas, his eldest. Mrs. Constance Garceau was my mother.

It did not name Agnes Brown, the mother who had borne him. It did not name Helen.

The notice gave the facts of a working life. The family remembered other things. His friends called him Doug. He was always impeccably dressed, his hair perfectly combed. He loved to read.

The same notice announced the funeral for ten o'clock on Monday morning, March 13, from the Ruth E. Urquhart funeral home at 812 Greenwich Avenue, Warwick.

He was buried at Saint Ann Cemetery in Cranston, under a stone that bears his name and Constance's. The cemetery index places that grave in section 5, lot 84, the lot where Constance Darcy Douglas's brother, Albert Norman Darcy, had been buried in 1954. The stone reads:

LAURENCE B. DOUGLAS
1907–1961

Between the first name and the name of the family that raised him, the stone keeps a single letter: B, for Brown. Thirty-three years later the same stone would carry his wife's name too.

chapters.label: Epilogue
chapters.title: The Names He Carried
chapters.html:
He was gone, but the people he had loved went on.

Constance Darcy Douglas was forty-eight when her husband died. She kept nursing. In 1963 the Warwick directory lists her as Constance, widow of Lawrence B., nurse, at 119 Phillips Avenue, Warwick. In 1965 she was at 1292 Post Road, Warwick, a nurse at the Briarcliffe Health Center in Johnston. Later she worked eight years at Cranston General Hospital, and she retired in 1974. Her mother, Eugenie Delaire Darcy, died in 1966 and was buried in the same section at Saint Ann.

In her last years Constance Darcy Douglas lived on Sixth Street in East Greenwich and went to St. Francis de Sales Church. The family remembers her pleasant, congenial nature. We, her grandchildren, called her Nan. She died at Rhode Island Hospital, Providence, on Tuesday, April 12, 1994, at eighty-one, leaving three daughters, twelve grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. She was buried with Laurence at Saint Ann, in lot 84, grave 3, thirty-three years after him, and her name is on the stone beside his.

Janet Page Douglas Crombie, Robert and Elizabeth Douglas's own daughter and seven years older than Laurence, who had sailed with him on the Duchess of Bedford in 1929 and whose Chicago address he gave as his own when he married in 1939, died in December 1979, aged seventy-nine. Her last residence was Maywood, Illinois. Her twin daughters, Betty and Jessie, died in 2009 and 2015.

Helen Ena Harrison, the soldier's daughter born at Bareilly, registered as an alien at Newton, Massachusetts, sometime in the early 1940s, under registration number A4384659. The index lists her as Helen E. Douglas, with a companion entry as Helen E. Harrison; her surviving immigration file carries the name Helen Harrison. Her younger brother, Alexander Edward Harrison, of Aveley, Essex, died in 1966.

In the end Helen went home to Ayr. By 1950 she was working as a secretary for the National Coal Board and living at 1a Inverkar Road, her parents' house. On Friday, August 11, 1950, in Ayr, by the forms of the Church of Scotland, she married George Lees Pirrie, a grocer's assistant and a widower, six years younger than she was. The register describes her as formerly married to Laurence Brown Douglas, against whom she had obtained a decree of divorce. She had divorced one grocer's assistant and married another. They made their home at 1a Inverkar Road, where her mother died two years later. She died there at ten past ten on the morning of Friday, March 16, 1973, of a cerebral thrombosis, a stroke, brought on by hardening of the arteries. She was sixty-five. George Pirrie, her widower, registered the death the same day; by then he worked as a sales assistant in a department store. The register lists both her husbands. The first is "Laurence Brown Douglas, Grocer (Assistant)." Forty-three years after the wedding in Chicago, and twelve years after his death, the record of her death still gave him his full name, Brown and Douglas together.

Agnes McGarth Brown, who gave birth to him in Edinburgh on the evening of June 14, 1907, registered him as Lawrence Brown, and gave him the first name of her uncle Lawrence, married Thomas McKenzie in 1911 and had two daughters, Mary and Jean. One portrait of her is known, a head-and-shoulders picture that the descendant who shared it describes as cropped from a full-length photograph in which she holds a rolled paper.

He had been born in the last years of peace before the First World War and grew up in a town that sent its men to the trenches. He crossed the ocean between the wars and married as the second began. In the autumn of 1941 he went east to work in Pennsylvania while his wife and family stayed in San Francisco, and he became an American in the middle of the war. He lived out his last years under the shadow of the next one. War ran through his life as it ran through the lives of his generation.

He carried more than one name. He was born Lawrence Brown, the son of Agnes. He grew up Laurence Douglas, in the family of Robert and Elizabeth. He crossed the ocean as Lawrence Brown again. In 1943, in a federal court in Pittsburgh, he became a citizen of the United States as Laurence Brown Douglas: both names at once, the mother who bore him and the family that raised him.
